item.title: Congressional Democrats plan Oman war powers push after Trump threatens bombing
item.description:
Congressional Democrats are planning a new push to constrain President Trump's war powers after he threatened Monday to "bomb the shit" out of Oman.

Why it matters: War powers resolutions, though largely symbolic, have become Democrats' go-to tool for trying to rein in what they see as a far too trigger-happy administration.

  • "At this point we may just need to file war powers resolutions for the 192 other countries," Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Axios.

Driving the news: Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) announced in a statement on Monday afternoon that he will introduce an Oman war powers resolution when the Senate returns to session next month.

  • Kaine noted that the the U.S. "has a strong diplomatic relationship and a free trade agreement" with Oman and argued that Trump's threats work to the benefit of "real adversaries" such as Russia and China.
  • The Virginia Democrat said he hopes to "find some Republican colleagues to join with Democrats and check this blindly stumbling power-drunk President from inflicting more damage on the U.S. and the world."

The other side: "Politicians in the United States and around the world have been talking about the danger posed by a nuclear Iran for decades. Only President Trump, however, has possessed the courage to take this national security threat head-on," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement to Axios.

  • "The administration has been fully transparent with Congress over the course of this conflict and throughout negotiations, and senior officials have provided over 30 bipartisan briefings to the Hill since late February."
  • "The Iranian regime – which for 47 years has chanted 'Death to America' and threatened our troops overseas – can never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon."

Catch up quick: Trump issued his threat to the gulf country, an American ally which has been involved in efforts to broker a deal to end the U.S.-Iran war, in an interview with Fox News.

  • "If Oman gets in the way" of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the president said in the phone interview, "we'll bomb the shit out of them."
  • Asked by reporters later on Monday if he is out of patience with Oman, Trump said, "I don't think they've behaved very well, but we'd handle them very easily, just like we do other things."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with White House comment.

item.title: Kindergarten vaccine exemptions rose in 2025-2026: CDC
item.description:
Vaccination rates among American kindergartners decreased during the 2025–2026 school year for all tracked vaccines, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported on Monday.

  • Exemptions from getting one or more vaccines increased in 41 states and the District of Columbia, growing to 4.2% from 3.6% the year before.

Why it matters: The drop-off coincided with continued efforts by the Trump administration to make controversial vaccine policy changes and with measles cases hitting levels not seen in more than three decades.

By the numbers: Coverage with the MMR, DTaP, polio and varicella vaccine decreased in more than half of states, ranging from 92% for diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine to 92.4% for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and polio vaccines. Public health officials say overall measles vaccination rates should remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity.

  • The number of kindergartners attending school without documentation of completing the two-dose MMR vaccine series was about 280,000 in 2025–2026, officials said.
  • The number of kindergartners exempt from one or more vaccines was about 155,000.
  • 24 states reported exemptions exceeding 5%.

MMR vaccine coverage among kindergartners by state ranged from 98.9% in West Virginia to 75.2% in Idaho.

What they're saying: The CDC, in a statement, said the data showed a 0.1% decline in vaccination coverage among children entering kindergarten.

  • The agency said it continues to encourage parents to discuss vaccination options with their doctors.

Yes, but: It only takes a small drop in the vaccination rate to make herd immunity against measles plummet.

  • The new data also doesn't indicate how many community clusters may actually have seen much greater declines.

Between the lines: Polling shows childhood vaccines remain popular, but administration efforts to upend longstanding vaccine policies could further erode trust in vaccines and public health, medical experts say.

  • President Trump last week signed an executive order calling for a slimmed-down childhood vaccine schedule and breaking the MMR vaccine into three separately administered shots.
  • It also advises states to review federal vaccine recommendations and update their requirements for school enrollment.
  • Capital Alpha Partners analyst Kim Monk wrote in a note Monday that any official vaccine scheduling recommendations or policy changes stemming from the order are expected to be challenged in court.
  • "As with past administration attempts to change or influence vaccine schedules, we think it's likely that providers and stakeholder groups will continue to ignore this advice, although these developments certainly don't help with ongoing vaccine hesitancy," Monk wrote.

item.title: Middle East demands are testing America's Pacific presence
item.description:
The USS George Washington's deployment from Japan to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln will leave the U.S. without an aircraft carrier in the western Pacific — just as adversaries in the area are flexing their military power.

Why it matters: Temporary carrier gaps are not uncommon, but the absence of a striker ship in the Pacific highlights how the Middle East is once again dictating American military policy. It also has raised questions about how the U.S. can sustain a formidable presence in both regions.

The big picture: The absence of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific has happened before, and China has previously exploited those gaps by sailing its strike groups closer to U.S. allies like Taiwan and Japan, Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Colonel and a current senior adviser at CSIS, tells Axios.

  • While a full-scale invasion is unlikely, China could use the void to ratchet up its presence in the Pacific, he says.
  • The region is crucial for the U.S. both militarily and economically, hosting at least 66 "significant defense sites," while Taiwan produces the majority of the chips America needs to run its AI industry.

Catch up quick: The Japan-based USS George Washington is heading to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose sailors have been deployed for about nine months and are reportedly dealing with mental health problems and supply disruptions.

By the numbers: The Navy has an 11-carrier fleet, which allows two carriers to be deployed continuously without burning out crews, Bryan Clark, a former submariner and current senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, tells Axios.

  • If two carriers stay stationed in the Middle East to support operations in Iran, then there will likely be months each year when the Pacific presence drops to zero.
  • Additionally, carriers will need maintenance and repairs after long deployments, which means they won't be available as often going forward, he says.
  • Clark says the 11-carrier fleet is still sufficient for U.S. defense — but only if deployments are managed carefully.

Between the lines: The carrier departure coincides with Trump "substantially" trimming routine joint U.S.-South Korea military drills and preparing for an upcoming summit with Xi Jinping in China.

  • While the administration is not formally retreating from the Indo-Pacific, the combination of a carrier gap and reduced military exercises could reinforce Beijing's argument that U.S. security commitments are unreliable.

What they're saying: "The United States military maintains the force posture necessary to achieve any desired objective set by the Commander-in-Chief," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "As Operation Epic Fury demonstrated, America's military might is stronger than it's ever been."

Zoom out: "If you are Taiwan or the Philippines or Japan, you're looking at this and saying the U.S. is basically not here, and the Chinese are, and the Chinese are showing off their military capability," Clark says.

  • If the pattern continues, Clark says, countries in the region could begin questioning whether Washington would actually be supportive in a crisis.
  • "The Chinese don't even have to fight a war if they can convince those neighbors that the U.S. really isn't going to be there for them, and that they should just bandwagon with China and go along with what China wants to do."

Go deeper: Trump shrugs off concerns about dismal conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln

item.title: Big Bend border wall construction paused by Trump administration
item.description:
The Trump administration paused border wall construction at Big Bend National Park in Texas while U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott visits the site, Scott announced Monday.

Why it matters: The wall's construction inside the national park has been the subject of bipartisan pushback and criticism that the job has been rushed, and is damaging to the environment.

Driving the news: "Last night, I put a pause on all activity in that park as far as construction goes till I can get down there and do a personal evaluation, talk to some stakeholders, talk to some local law enforcement in that area," Scott said in a video posted to X.

  • "More to follow this week."

Catch up quick: The Trump administration has pushed to quickly expand the border wall as part of its effort to reduce unauthorized immigration across the border with Mexico.

  • Earlier this year, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem signed at least 28 environmental and cultural preservation waivers to speed up the project.
  • The government has threatened to seize land if property owners don't grant access.

Zoom in: Scott said CBP is "firmly committed to protecting America, and that includes our national treasures like Big Bend National Park (BBNP)."

  • "We know the current and predictable national security threats and they are real," he said, adding that his evaluation will ensure America secures its borders "while simultaneously protecting BBNP for generations to come."

Zoom out: Despite containing about 517 miles of the Southern border along the Rio Grande, the Big Bend region accounts for a tiny fraction of border crossings because of its rugged terrain.

Go deeper: Inside the unbuilding of Trump's border wall

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: House Ethics investigating Rep. Jimmy Gomez over sexual misconduct allegations
item.description:
The House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it is investigating Congressman Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) over allegations of sexual misconduct.

Why it matters: Gomez is the latest House member to face scrutiny over alleged sexual misconduct amid a string of incidents that have prompted calls to tighten Congress' rules.

  • Gomez said in a statement that he's made "personal mistakes outside my marriage," but said his actions were "consensual" and did not violate the law or House Ethics rules.
  • "I take full responsibility and have committed myself to working through the pain privately with my wife and family. I sought professional assistance to help re-center and heal my relationships and move forward with honesty, transparency, and respect," Gomez said, adding he plans to cooperate with the committee's probe.

Driving the news: The committee said in a statement that it is reviewing allegations that Gomez "engaged in sexual misconduct in violation of the Code of Official Conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct, including engaging in inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer."

  • The committee provided no further details about the allegations.
  • CNN reported in June that the panel was investigating Gomez, including over an alleged romantic relationship he had in 2023 with an aide who worked for another member of Congress. Gomez, 51, has been married since 2011.

The big picture: House rules do not currently bar members of Congress from having relationships with staffers outside their own offices, but the bipartisan sexual misconduct task force is weighing whether to recommend banning all lawmaker-staffer sexual relationships.

  • House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) endorsed such a ban last month, telling Axios: "I think it's inappropriate, as it would be in any workplace."

Zoom out: Congress has faced a series of sexual misconduct scandals and investigations this year.

  • Two lawmakers — Reps. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) and Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) — resigned earlier this year amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Swalwell also faces allegations of sexual assault. Swalwell has denied the allegations. Gonzales admitted to an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide.
  • Ethics concluded that Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) violated House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment, and recommended his censure earlier this month. Edwards has denied any wrongdoing.
  • Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) is also under an Ethics investigation for allegations that center on domestic abuse, stolen valor and financial misconduct, all of which he denies.

The bottom line: The Ethics panel's investigations can take months, sometimes years, to yield formal reports or disciplinary recommendations.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from Rep. Gomez.

item.title: Kushner urges Netanyahu to test Hamas disarmament in Gaza
item.description:
President Trump adviser Jared Kushner told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday that the U.S. wants Israel to take "small steps" in Gaza to test whether Hamas' commitment to start disarming is genuine, a U.S. official said.

Why it matters: The four-hour meeting took place amid deep skepticism from Netanyahu about the U.S. plan for Gaza — and ahead of an October election that makes the Israeli leader reluctant to offer significant concessions on the politically sensitive issue.

  • While the meeting helped clarify misunderstandings, addressed some of Netanyahu's concerns and produced a joint understanding on how to move forward, it also crystallized the remaining differences and made clear how difficult near-term progress will be.

Driving the news: Kushner arrived in Israel after meetings in Egypt Sunday with Hamas leaders and with the Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators.

  • Kushner brought a delegation to the meeting with Netanyahu that included the High Representative of Trump's Gaza Board of Peace, Nikolay Mladenov, as well as former British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Board of Peace senior advisers Aryeh Lightstone and Liran Tancman.
  • During the meeting, Netanyahu expressed deep skepticism about Hamas' commitment to demilitarize and asked Kushner why he met with its leaders in Egypt on Sunday.
  • Kushner told Netanyahu it was important to hear from them directly on whether they're willing to move forward with demilitarization, a U.S. official said.
  • "The last time Steve Witkoff and I met with Hamas leaders, it led to the release of all the hostages," Kushner told Netanyahu, according to a U.S. official. He was referring to the release last year of the remaining hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks.

The big picture: A U.S. official and another source with knowledge of the meeting said the political atmosphere in Israel ahead of the October election has created significant suspicion on the Israeli side — particularly as the Israeli opposition has attacked Netanyahu for making concessions in Gaza.

  • Much of the meeting focused on explaining the Board of Peace plan, clarifying misconceptions and addressing Netanyahu's concerns, the U.S. official and the second source said.
  • During the meeting, Netanyahu showed Kushner two public opinion polls. One showed that a majority of Israelis object to the reconstruction of Gaza before the enclave is demilitarized. Another found that most Israelis want to continue strikes against imminent threats in Gaza.
  • The U.S. official said Kushner told Netanyahu the U.S. doesn't expect Israel to refrain from taking action against imminent threats by Hamas. He stressed that the plan from Trump's Board of Peace calls for the reconstruction process to begin only after demilitarization is concluded.

Zoom in: Kushner said the demilitarization process would work like this: First, Hamas would hand over its weapons to the Palestinian technocratic government, which would give them to an International Stabilization Force. That force would destroy the weapons, the U.S. official said.

  • Netanyahu had the heads of Israeli military intelligence and the Shin Bet intelligence agency brief Kushner and his team on Hamas violations.

Friction point: While Kushner and Netanyahu were meeting, Trump told Fox News that he wants Israel to stop its airstrikes in Gaza.

  • A Board of Peace official said Trump was pointing to strikes that are not against imminent threats.
  • How to define an imminent threat is a key point of difference between the Board of Peace and the Israeli government. The issue still needs to be addressed, a Board of Peace official said.
  • A U.S. official said Kushner and Netanyahu agreed to form a "deconfliction" mechanism in Gaza that would monitor violations and address Israeli concerns about emerging threats to prevent escalation on the ground. Egyptian mediators would be involved, the U.S. official said.
  • "If the Israelis see Hamas doing something that could be an emerging threat, they will report it to the deconfliction mechanism and it will bring it up with Hamas. This way Hamas will know we are watching them," the U.S. official said.

Zoom out: The U.S. official said Netanyahu committed to taking steps to improve the humanitarian situation in Gaza, especially when it comes to water and sanitation.

  • Kushner and Netanyahu agreed to form two working groups — one on demilitarization of Gaza and another on the humanitarian situation.
  • "The gaps with the Israelis are not that great. None of us is relying on trusting Hamas," the U.S. official said. "But we think we can start doing some tangible steps. There is a ton of fearmongering as part of the political atmosphere in Israel. But if we see weapons being handed over by Hamas, that would be the first sign it is real."
  • In a statement after the meeting, Netanyahu's office referred to the two working groups and noted that demilitarization would need to be completed "before reconstruction begins."
  • A Board of Peace official said the meeting was "lengthy, in depth, and very productive. We agreed with [Netanyahu] on a path forward. The Israelis are going to give this a chance. Now it's up to Hamas to show if it truly intends to comply."

item.title: Trump fails to undo E. Jean Carroll verdict at Supreme Court
item.description:
The Supreme Court once again declined to take up President Trump's attempt to toss a jury's $5 million finding that he sexually abused and defamed E. Jean Carroll.

The big picture: Carroll's payday had been long delayed as the president fought the verdict. The Supreme Court already declined to throw it out earlier this year.

  • Trump's lawyers are also still fighting a separate $83.3 million defamation judgment he was ordered to pay her, arguing he's entitled to presidential immunity.

Driving the news: The justices did not explain their reasoning for declining to take up the challenge, as is typical.

  • After the Supreme Court rejected Trump's bid to toss the civil verdict in late June, his legal team petitioned for a rehearing, pointing to his separate challenge over immunity claims.
  • Carroll received the more than $5 million she was owed earlier this year, which her legal team said she would place in an interest-bearing account until Trump's petition was denied.

What they're saying: A spokesman for Trump's legal team slammed what he described as the "Democrat-funded travesty of the Carroll Hoaxes" in a statement provided to Axios.

  • Roberta Kaplan, Carroll's attorney, applauded the Supreme Court's rejection, noting that "[a]s a result, the jury's unanimous verdict that Donald Trump sexually assaulted and then defamed E. Jean Carroll is now final and cannot be challenged in any court."

Catch up quick: Carroll filed two lawsuits against Trump stemming from her allegation that he sexually assaulted her in a New York department store in the mid-1990s and his subsequent denials.

  • She first sued him in 2019 for defamation over statements he made accusing her of fabricating the claim.
  • She sued him again in 2022, this time alleging sexual assault and defamation for another statement Trump made. That second lawsuit went to trial first, and in May 2023, a jury found Trump liable, awarding her $5 million.
  • A jury in the other lawsuit then awarded Carroll $83.3 million for Trump's defamation. His lawyers unsuccessfully appealed the $83.3 million judgment to a federal appeals court.
  • But the president's team is now asking the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing presidential immunity shield Trump from liability for statements he made while president, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reported.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Older Democrats walloped by midterms anti-establishment revolt
item.description:
House Democrats who have comfortably held their seats for decades are suddenly finding the ground shifting beneath their feet as primary voters revolt against the party's old guard.

Why it matters: The anti-establishment revolution that has swept Democratic primaries this year is poised to drastically alter the makeup of the party caucus and Congress as a whole.

  • Rep. John Larson (D-Conn.) became the latest victim of this trend: The 78-year-old lost his primary by more than 20 percentage points to 47-year-old former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin.
  • Larson emerged as a top target for the Democratic youth brigade after he suffered a highly publicized freeze-up during a House floor speech last year that he later said was due to a complex partial seizure.

By the numbers: Larson is one of seven House Democrats who have lost their primaries this year — five of whom are past retirement age.

  • Reps. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), 69, Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), 71, and Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.), 71, all lost challenges to younger opponents affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America.
  • Rep. Al Green (D-Texas), 78, lost to 38-year-old freshman Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) after the two were placed in the same seat by GOP-led mid-decade redistricting.
  • These losses, along with the ousters of Reps. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) and Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.), make 2026 tied with 2012 as the worst year for Democratic incumbents in primaries in the 21st century.

What they're saying: "Democratic voters are hungry for a new generation of leaders who can credibly argue they'll fight for change," Amanda Litman, founder of progressive group Run For Something, told Axios.

  • Bronin's defeat of Larson — who positioned himself as the progressive in the race — shows that "'sick of the status quo' cuts across ideological lines," Litman said.
  • "We have a generation of younger people who are fed up," former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg, whose group Leaders We Deserve has been supporting many of these primary challenges, said in an interview.
  • Hogg added: "Generational change and the change of the status quo is the story of the cycle."

The other side: "200 Democrats are running for reelection in primaries and almost every one of them had a younger challenger," Rep. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), 71, told Axios.

  • Sherman, who easily dispatched a well-funded challenge from 42-year-old former Biden administration official Jake Levine this year, said he has "always had a younger challenger, it's just not a race that you notice."
  • "You're only going to focus on the five or 10 where the younger challenger got close or won," he said.

What we're hearing: A senior House Democrat, asked how Sherman survived while Larson lost, said Larson "didn't work [his] district hard" while Sherman "worked his district."

  • "People are demanding change," acknowledged another senior House Democrat. "I personally think members should retire at 75."

Between the lines: A clear trend noted by both Hogg and Sherman is that challengers who focused their message on generational change tended to fare worse than those who added left-wing policy positions to the mix.

  • In addition to Sherman, Reps. Mike Thompson (D-Calif.), 75, and Ed Case (D-Hawaii), 73, both put up surprisingly strong performances against well-funded, younger challengers who campaigned as traditional Democrats.
  • Said Hogg: "I don't think running ... as a generational change candidate and basically saying, 'I'm young, but I want more of the status quo,' is not a winning message, obviously."

One dynamic that kept 2026 from being an even worse year for House Democrats whose old age had become a distinct liability is that a huge cohort of them opted to retire rather than face a grueling primary.

  • Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-N.Y.), 79, and Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.) 89, had insisted they were running for reelection before bowing to pressure to drop out.
  • Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.) pursued reelection but died at 80-years-old just a month before he was set to face several primary challengers.
  • "Look, Eleanor Holmes Norton, a year ago, wanted to run for reelection, and she had reached a time in life when it was time to retire," said Sherman. "In Congress, you're either going to voluntarily retire or you're going to lose.

Several others, including Reps. Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.), 77, and Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), 79, were forced out of their seats by mid-decade redistricting.

  • Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), 86, and former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), 87, opted for voluntary retirement.
  • So did Reps. Danny Davis (D-Ill.), 84, Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.), 83, Jan Schakowsky (D-Ill.), 82, Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), 73, and Dwight Evans (D-Pa.), 72.

What's next: Democrats' youth guard is hoping for a few more victories this cycle, with Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), 80, and Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), 71, both trying to fend off challengers.

  • Hogg said he thinks Markey will prevail over his more moderate challenger, 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), telling Axios: "I don't think Seth Moulton is going to win."
  • His group is more excited about Patrick Roath, the progressive 39-year-old attorney running against Lynch, a centrist.
  • Thompson and Rep. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.), 81, both have to win November runoffs against their younger Democratic opponents as well. "Matsui has to worry," the first senior House Democrat said.

The bottom line: Just because an older member survived their primary this year doesn't mean they will in the 2028 election cycle.

  • Said Litman: "I expect that even the challengers who lost will be back for another run in the future — they've built infrastructure and name recognition that will help them in the future."

Editor's note: This story has been updated to include Rep. Steve Cohen's age and to clarify that he dropped out due to redistricting.

item.title: Birding, silent book club, Mahjong and more: America's meetup explosion
item.description:
Young people raised on swiping, DMing and streaming are doing something bold: going out.

Why it matters: Amid a loneliness epidemic, millennials and Gen Zers are craving IRL connection — enough to show up for meetups built around activities once considered solitary, or "grandma hobbies."

The latest: They're leaving the house to play chess, birdwatch and read in silence together.

  • "It's very easy to sit inside and rot just by yourself," Cole Robinson, president of the Audubon on Campus Trinity University chapter, tells Axios San Antonio.
  • But activities like birding can help you "feel a little less lonely," the 20-year-old says.

"Soft socializing" experiences — where you're with other people but networking is not the main focus — have taken off, per Eventbrite.

By the numbers: There were 151% more puzzle competitions from August 2024 to July 2025, compared to the preceding 12 months, according to Eventbrite numbers (separate from the below "singles" data) shared with Axios.

  • And mahjong-focused events are up 94% earlier this year compared to last, according to Evite data shared with Axios.
Data: Eventbrite; Chart: Brad Jennings/Axios; Note: U.S. Eventbrite data for in-person, publicly listed events including connection-oriented language in their descriptions.

The big picture: The trend extends to finding love, too. Americans are seeking romantic connection at so-called "meet-cute" events — settings meant to spark a sweet "How'd you meet?" story, away from apps.

  • The meetups can revolve around trivia, Powerpoint presentations, crafts and even exercise.

Meanwhile, platonic dinner parties with strangers have also gained traction.

  • Axios just launched our own dinner series, bringing readers together for our new Axios Social Club starting in Charlotte, Chicago, Kansas City and San Antonio.

"Everybody's been stuck behind their phones for the past two decades, and it's not good for humanity," writer Stuart Schuffman — who recently launched an IRL dinner club for his Broke-Ass Stuart readers — tells Axios San Francisco.

  • People "want more connection and less doomscrolling," he says.

item.title: Why prescription drug prices are plunging
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

America is experiencing its biggest prescription drug price deflation in generations.

Why it matters: By one important measure, there is a striking reversal underway for one of health care's most stubbornly expensive necessities amid a major Washington push to lower drug costs.

By the numbers: Prescription drug prices fell 0.8% in July and are down 3.1% from a year ago — the steepest annual decline in more than six decades, according to the recent Consumer Price Index.

  • Prices haven't risen in any month this year, an unusually persistent stretch of flat or falling drug prices.
  • The downward trend comes as costs for hospital and physician services continue to rise.

The intrigue: Trump administration officials are taking a victory lap for the price drop, although TrumpRx — the administration's website connecting patients with discounted cash prices for certain drugs — likely only accounts for part of the decline.

  • Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk also struck deals with the administration that cut cash prices for blockbuster GLP-1 drugs and expanded Medicare access.
  • Those cuts may have added to broader downward pressure on drug prices, though other forces were already at work.

Another potential factor: Medicare negotiations established under the Inflation Reduction Act took effect in January for 10 of the program's costliest drugs, with negotiated prices as much as 79% below their list prices.

Zoom in: Changes in what Medicare pays pharmacies can show up in the prescription drug CPI.

  • The government tracks the prices that pharmacies receive from patients and insurers, including Medicare, not just what consumers pay out of pocket.
  • Manufacturer rebates paid after the transaction are not captured in the index, the Bureau of Labor Statistics told Axios.

What they're saying: Geoffrey Joyce, a USC health economist, said that TrumpRx makes discounts easier to find but often points consumers to prices that already exist.

  • "If you were going to give policy credit, you'd have to say the IRA," Joyce said. Still, he added, much of the decline is being driven by market forces.

The big picture: As blockbuster drugs lose patent protection, cheaper generics enter the market, a shift the government's inflation gauge is designed to capture.

  • Heated competition in the market for GLP-1 drugs is pushing down cash-pay prices.

The other side: White House spokesperson Kush Desai called attributing the decline to the IRA "idiotic and unfounded," arguing that its negotiated prices failed to deliver meaningful savings beyond existing insurer discounts.

  • Desai pointed instead to Trump's most-favored-nation deals, aimed at aligning U.S. drug prices with lower prices overseas, and discounts available through TrumpRx.

What we're watching: Falling prices in the aggregate do not necessarily translate into relief for consumers, given the complexity of drug pricing and payments.

  • Six in 10 Americans this spring said they were worried about affording their medications, according to KFF — the largest share since the group began tracking the question in 2018.
  • Four in 10 said that in the past year they hadn't taken medication as prescribed because of cost.
  • "People don't care about what the true cost of the drug is," Joyce said. "They just say, 'What's my copay?' or 'What's my cost sharing at the pharmacy counter?'"

Caitlin Owens and Adriel Bettelheim contributed reporting.

Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

America is experiencing its biggest prescription drug price deflation in generations.

Why it matters: By one important measure, there is a striking reversal underway for one of health care's most stubbornly expensive necessities amid a major Washington push to lower drug costs.

By the numbers: Prescription drug prices fell 0.8% in July and are down 3.1% from a year ago — the steepest annual decline in more than six decades, according to the recent Consumer Price Index.

  • Prices haven't risen in any month this year, an unusually persistent stretch of flat or falling drug prices.
  • The downward trend comes as costs for hospital and physician services continue to rise.

The intrigue: Trump administration officials are taking a victory lap for the price drop, although TrumpRx — the administration's website connecting patients with discounted cash prices for certain drugs — likely only accounts for part of the decline.

  • Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk also struck deals with the administration that cut cash prices for blockbuster GLP-1 drugs and expanded Medicare access.
  • Those cuts may have added to broader downward pressure on drug prices, though other forces were already at work.

Another potential factor: Medicare negotiations established under the Inflation Reduction Act took effect in January for 10 of the program's costliest drugs, with negotiated prices as much as 79% below their list prices.

Zoom in: Changes in what Medicare pays pharmacies can show up in the prescription drug CPI.

  • The government tracks the prices that pharmacies receive from patients and insurers, including Medicare, not just what consumers pay out of pocket.
  • Manufacturer rebates paid after the transaction are not captured in the index, the Bureau of Labor Statistics told Axios.

What they're saying: Geoffrey Joyce, a USC health economist, said that TrumpRx makes discounts easier to find but often points consumers to prices that already exist.

  • "If you were going to give policy credit, you'd have to say the IRA," Joyce said. Still, he added, much of the decline is being driven by market forces.

The big picture: As blockbuster drugs lose patent protection, cheaper generics enter the market, a shift the government's inflation gauge is designed to capture.

  • Heated competition in the market for GLP-1 drugs is pushing down cash-pay prices.

The other side: White House spokesperson Kush Desai called attributing the decline to the IRA "idiotic and unfounded," arguing that its negotiated prices failed to deliver meaningful savings beyond existing insurer discounts.

  • Desai pointed instead to Trump's most-favored-nation deals, aimed at aligning U.S. drug prices with lower prices overseas, and discounts available through TrumpRx.

What we're watching: Falling prices in the aggregate do not necessarily translate into relief for consumers, given the complexity of drug pricing and payments.

  • Six in 10 Americans this spring said they were worried about affording their medications, according to KFF — the largest share since the group began tracking the question in 2018.
  • Four in 10 said that in the past year they hadn't taken medication as prescribed because of cost.
  • "People don't care about what the true cost of the drug is," Joyce said. "They just say, 'What's my copay?' or 'What's my cost sharing at the pharmacy counter?'"

Caitlin Owens and Adriel Bettelheim contributed reporting.

item.title: The Democratic establishment's ideas deficit
item.description:
The centrist Democratic group Third Way recently declared "war" on democratic socialists to head off what they fear could be a far-left hijacking of the party ahead of 2028.

  • But establishment Democrats have made clear what they're against without making much of a case for what they're for.

Why it matters: It's hard to beat something with nothing.

  • Democratic socialism, whatever you think of it, is easy to grasp: Tax billionaires and redistribute wealth. Provide government-funded health care and child care for everyone. Rely less on markets for housing and education. Empower workers with stronger unions.
  • The establishment vision is murky. Raise taxes, but not too high; use government to make health care and child care more affordable, rather than taking them over; rein in the excesses of capitalism without upending capitalism itself.
  • That's a tougher vision to sum up, let alone rally behind.
  • "Without question, we agree with the left that we have failed to convince working-class voters that their lives will be better if they put us in charge," Third Way co-founder Matt Bennett told Axios. "You'd have to be insane to disagree."

State of play: A string of democratic socialist wins in House primaries, followed by progressive Abdul El-Sayed's win in the Michigan Senate primary, has set off a debate over whether the Democratic Party is undergoing a transformation.

  • New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the most prominent democratic socialist, is emerging as a formidable potential presidential candidate in 2028.
  • But others argue the party hasn't fundamentally changed from 2020. That year, Joe Biden dispatched a primary field that lurched left on health care, crime and immigration (though Biden also adapted to accommodate the party's leftward shift).
  • "Give progressives credit for bringing ideas to the table. Pragmatists haven't been as good as we need to be about offering our own ideas and agenda," potential Democratic presidential candidate Rahm Emanuel wrote on X.
  • But, pointing to democratic socialist Francesca Hong's loss in her primary for Wisconsin governor and other mainstream Democrats winning the same night, he added: "[T]he pragmatic wing isn't a faction of this party. It's the majority, it's awake now, and it's exerting itself."

Between the lines: Third Way recently announced a $15 million campaign to take on the progressive left.

  • Bennett said Third Way has 100-plus people working on a policy menu — a "new kind of offer for working-class voters who have abandoned Democrats" — that he hopes 2028 Democrats will draw from.
  • There are already clear examples of centrists drawing a bright line with democratic socialists, he added. "Where we strongly differ with them is around the particulars. They're for Medicare for all, and we're for … a health care bill of rights that would improve the existing system, not throw it out and replace it with a $30 trillion socialization of the health care space."

Yes, but: Some liberals have tried to chart a fresh direction for the party. Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argued in a 2025 book that Democrats should become the party of "abundance" — building more housing, infrastructure and clean energy — by cutting red tape and making government work better.

  • But it hasn't caught fire.

The big picture: Some middle-of-the-road Democrats say the problem isn't just about ideas — it's also about tone.

  • Their argument: Voters want fighters to take on President Trump, but the party establishment — unlike progressives — too often offers split-the-difference responses.
  • Third Way President Jon Cowan, speaking at a Democratic Party strategy summit in March, called instead for a "combative" centrism.

The bottom line: Establishment Democrats have lost their identity. 2028 will show whether they can give voters something to rally around — or whether the party has moved away from them.

item.title: How wildfires are changing the U.S. electric grid
item.description:
Years of destructive fires are forcing utilities to prioritize wildfire resilience as they plan the next generation of the U.S. electric grid.

Why it matters: Utilities aren't just expanding the electric grid — they're designing it to withstand a more fire-prone climate.

  • This year's wildfire season is exceeding the 10-year average for both the number of fires and acres burned.

The big picture: The U.S. is embarking on one of the biggest grid expansions in decades just as wildfire risk is becoming a defining challenge for utilities. Today's planning decisions may determine how resilient tomorrow's grid becomes.

  • Utilities are combining weather models, wildfire behavior, infrastructure data and population impacts to help prioritize resilience investments, Nadia Panossian, an electrical engineering researcher at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, tells Axios.
  • Undergrounding — burying power lines underground — can also improve resilience to hurricanes, winter storms and other hazards, Seth Guikema, a University of Michigan professor of civil and environmental engineering, tells Axios.
  • He says utilities also have to manage aging infrastructure, which in many cases is "the bigger challenge than building new."

State of play: Wildfires are already affecting how utilities operate.

  • They disrupt the power system by damaging equipment, forcing utilities to cut power, and reducing solar generation when smoke blocks sunlight.

Yes, but: Preventing outages is no longer enough. Utilities now have to incorporate wildfire resilience into grid projects.

Case in point: California was one of the first states to require investor-owned utilities to publish wildfire resilience plans, Panossian says.

  • Other states have adopted similar approaches as wildfire risk grows.
  • Panossian says utilities are moving beyond "basic minimum maintenance" toward longer-term upgrades that account for future wildfire risks.
  • Some California utilities are already experimenting with microgrids that can disconnect from the main grid and keep supplying power during outages as wildfire risk grows, Guikema says.
  • But those investments "can be cost-prohibitive — and that's the challenge," he adds.

Catch up quick: Utilities have already learned costly lessons about wildfires.

  • California utilities have spent billions on wildfire mitigation.
  • PG&E emerged from bankruptcy after Camp Fire-related liabilities.
  • Utilities across the West now conduct public safety power shutoffs. "They shut the power off because you'd rather have a short-term power outage than a catastrophic fire," Panossian says.

What we're watching: The grid is poised for a major expansion. The U.S. needs thousands of miles of new transmission to connect renewables, storage and data centers.

  • Much of the U.S. grid also needs to be replaced. As utilities evaluate those upgrades, Panossian says, they're looking for opportunities to build wildfire resilience into those projects.
  • Guikema says utility planning is, in many ways, a cost-risk trade-off. "How much are we willing to increase our utility rates to do undergrounding and things like that?" he says.
  • In some cases, he says, regulators — not utilities — are limiting resilience investments because of cost concerns.

The bottom line: California has shown utilities what wildfire planning looks like. As wildfire risk spreads beyond the West, those lessons are shaping how the next generation of the U.S. grid is built.

Go deeper: Federal lab cuts could hamper fire forecasting efforts

item.title: What happens to what you share with AI
item.description:
Imagine a chatbot built to keep you talking a little longer. To change your mind about something. Or persuade you to buy something.

  • Now imagine it could draw on everything it knows about you — including the fears, insecurities and private details you shared in conversation — to do it.

Why it matters: Few rules directly govern that scenario today, making AI companies' promises about how they use consumer data especially consequential.

The big picture: In the first installment of Axios' "What they know about you" series, published in 2019, we examined the information major tech companies collected about their users. In 2024, we followed up with a look at what consumer data AI companies use to train their systems.

  • This new series revisits those questions — and widens the lens. We'll examine not only whether a company uses consumer data to train future AI models, but also how it can use that data now: to personalize responses, retain a memory, recommend content or target advertising.

Driving the news: AI companies are seeking access to data beyond the chat window.

  • OpenAI last week announced an optional Computer History feature that lets ChatGPT retain a record of the apps and websites a person uses.
  • Google, meanwhile, said last month it will use photos and other material people upload through Search to train its AI systems by default, though users can opt out.
  • The upside is the potential for more useful, personalized AI. The trade-off is giving companies a broader and more continuous view of users' lives.

Between the lines: Chatbots can invite a kind of disclosure that search engines and social networks often do not.

  • People use them to ask about health, money, work and relationships — potentially creating a more intimate record of their concerns.
  • Meta, Google and OpenAI are all exploring different approaches to advertising on their chatbots.
  • If consumer AI follows the path of search and social media, advertising could become a far more significant part of the business — creating an incentive for chatbot makers to increase engagement.

What they're saying: "The AI era will increasingly be fueled by people voluntarily handing over their full digital lives to AI tools that promise to relieve their mental load or loneliness," Miranda Bogen, chief technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology, told Axios.

  • "The more a system knows about you, the easier it will be to make escalating requests for private details in a way that feels natural," Bogen said. "Without robust privacy protections, the incentive to monetize that knowledge will be hard to resist."

Zoom in: Company policies vary considerably. Apple, for example, offers the most private option with Apple Intelligence requests on a user's device.

  • It handles the requests it can on-device. For more demanding tasks, Apple uses Private Cloud Compute, a system it says uses data only to fulfill the request and does not make that content accessible to Apple.
  • That approach can limit how much of a user's history Apple can retain and use for ongoing personalization.
  • It does not apply when a user chooses to send a request to a third-party service, such as ChatGPT.

Meta, by contrast, stakes a far broader claim to user data in its privacy policy.

  • The company says it can use interactions with Meta AI to personalize content and ads across its services, including some interactions through its smart glasses.
  • Meta also says it does not use conversations about certain sensitive topics — including health, politics and religion — to personalize ads.
  • It has also begun rolling out an Incognito Chat mode for temporary, private Meta AI conversations. This system is designed to work similarly to Apple's — Meta's servers see the query only to provide an answer, with no data stored.

Zoom out: Other AI services fall somewhere between Apple's device-centered approach and Meta's broader data-use policies.

  • Some offer temporary chats that are not used for memory or model training.
  • There are services that only train on user data if users give permission, while others require a person to opt out to avoid having their data used for training.
  • Many services allow users to see the data that is stored and delete specific memories. Sometimes that's as easy as asking the chatbot not to remember a particular detail. Others have more complex mechanisms for editing memories.
  • And then some chatbots also have separate rules for health information, children's data or conversations shared with connected apps.

What we're watching: The key distinction is no longer whether a company trains on your prompts. It is whether those prompts can shape the system's understanding of you — and what else that understanding can be used to do.

The bottom line: The value of a personalized chatbot may be worth the privacy trade-off for many people. But consumers deserve to understand the bargain before they start talking.

item.title: Trump tells Hegseth to cut back U.S.-South Korea drills
item.description:
President Trump said Sunday he instructed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" U.S. military exercises with South Korea.

The big picture: Trump cited his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un for condemning the drills — and also noted on Truth Social that South Korea declined his request to help the U.S. denuclearize Iran.

What he's saying: "These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile," Trump wrote.

Context: The U.S. and South Korean militaries were due to start regular military drills on Monday in an exercise known as "Ulchi Freedom Shield."

  • The drills have been held annually under that name since 2022, though the U.S.-South Korea summertime exercises they evolved from date back decades.

Friction point: On Wednesday, North Korea conducted a ballistic missile test for the first time since June, which experts and military officials assessed as an apparent protest against the drills.

  • The U.S., Japan and South Korea condemned the missile launch.

What we're watching: The Japan-based USS George Washington is being redeployed from the Pacific to the Middle East, where it is expected to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln.

  • That leaves the U.S. without a Pacific aircraft carrier at the same time that Trump is scaling back from the Korean drills.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: How AOC is rewriting her own "Woke 1" history
item.description:
New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is laughing off "Woke 1." But she's carrying baggage from the 2020 era of cultural progressivism that some Democrats say is an obstacle to a future presidential run.

Why it matters: AOC's pivot to the cultural center — which she began to roll out last week in a high-profile ABC interview by saying, "Woke 1 was crazy" — is potential damage control for her past remarks about law enforcement, immigration and a range of social issues.

  • Ocasio-Cortez told ABC that the left's so-called excesses of that period were partly the result of the COVID pandemic and lockdowns.
  • But she made some of her most controversial remarks before the pandemic hit the U.S. in 2020.
  • "This is really going to be something that handicaps her, especially with demographics that are culturally more moderate," former Biden White House adviser Yemisi Egbewole told us, pointing to Black voters in the South who have a large voice in Democratic presidential primaries.

Flashback: In the early 2020s, Ocasio-Cortez was one of the most aggressive and well-known advocates for "defunding" the police — an idea that polls have long shown is not popular.

  • In the summer of 2020, she blasted New York City's government for proposing to cut its police department by only $1 billion.
  • "Defunding police means defunding police," she said then. "It does not mean budget tricks or funny math." She added: "The fight to defund policing continues."

In 2019, AOC posted on social media that "we need to have a real conversation about decarceration & prison abolition in this country."

  • She said that year that some marginalized groups "have no choice but to riot."
  • And she said at an event in 2021: "I want to abolish our carceral system that's designed to trap Black and brown men."

On immigration, Ocasio-Cortez sponsored a bill in 2021 and 2023 to decriminalize border crossings. Asked by the New Yorker in 2019 if she would get rid of the Department of Homeland Security, she said: "I think so. I think so."

  • She repeatedly used language en vogue in elite liberal circles, such as the gender-neutral term "Latinx" in the early 2020s — a word that surveys have found isn't used by the vast majority of Latino Americans.
  • She used the phrase "menstruating person" in 2021 to be inclusive of the transgender community.

Zoom out: AOC now has shifted her rhetoric but hasn't detailed where she currently stands on many of these politically fraught topics, or what made her change her views on "Woke 1."

  • Ocasio-Cortez's spokespeople didn't respond to several questions, including what her position is now on defunding the police, whether she supports decriminalizing the border, and if she thinks rioting is sometimes justified.
  • In her ABC interview, Ocasio-Cortez did say that she doesn't support some Democratic Socialists of America's proposals such as abolishing police and prisons, defunding the Department of Defense and granting amnesty to all immigrants.

The other side: Some Republicans argue that AOC would be a formidable presidential candidate despite her controversial positions in the past.

  • "To me, she's incredibly dangerous," said GOP pollster Brent Buchanan, noting that AOC has high name recognition and an impressive favorability rating for a nationally known figure who's faced years of attacks.
  • He shared his polling that shows Ocasio-Cortez is seen favorably by 39% of voters, compared with 42% who view her unfavorably — a rating similar to Secretary of State Marco Rubio's.
  • Ocasio-Cortez's recent cultural moderation "tells me she's a good politician, because she's doing it now instead of next year," Buchanan added.

Democratic strategist James Carville likewise praised AOC, telling us that "it's always been evident that she's more talented than the rest of them put together," a reference to other members of the "Squad" of House progressives.

  • Carville said AOC doesn't need to over-explain her changes of heart: "She can say: 'I'm grown,' and people understand that."

Wisconsin's recent gubernatorial primary showed how cultural progressivism can be an albatross for the left — even at a time when economic populism is gaining momentum.

  • Socialist Francesca Hong lost by just under 4,000 votes after struggling to explain why she previously had called to "cancel Thanksgiving."
  • AOC declined to endorse Hong — the latest sign of her move to the center.

The big picture: Ocasio-Cortez is far from the only Democratic politician who wants voters to forget about their past cultural positions from the early 2020s.

  • California Gov. Gavin Newsom said last year that "not one person ever in my office has ever used the word Latinx," though he repeatedly did so in 2020.
  • Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, meanwhile, have walked back their past support for defunding the police.

Axios' Marc Caputo contributed reporting.

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is laughing off "Woke 1." But she's carrying baggage from the 2020 era of cultural progressivism that some Democrats say is an obstacle to a future presidential run.

Why it matters: AOC's pivot to the cultural center — which she began to roll out last week in a high-profile ABC interview by saying, "Woke 1 was crazy" — is potential damage control for her past remarks about law enforcement, immigration and a range of social issues.

  • Ocasio-Cortez told ABC that the left's so-called excesses of that period were partly the result of the COVID pandemic and lockdowns.
  • But she made some of her most controversial remarks before the pandemic hit the U.S. in 2020.
  • "This is really going to be something that handicaps her, especially with demographics that are culturally more moderate," former Biden White House adviser Yemisi Egbewole told us, pointing to Black voters in the South who have a large voice in Democratic presidential primaries.

Flashback: In the early 2020s, Ocasio-Cortez was one of the most aggressive and well-known advocates for "defunding" the police — an idea that polls have long shown is not popular.

  • In the summer of 2020, she blasted New York City's government for proposing to cut its police department by only $1 billion.

  • She said that year that some marginalized groups "have no choice but to riot."

item.title: Inside Kushner's Hamas meeting: What comes next in Gaza
item.description:
Hamas leaders reaffirmed their commitment to disarm and demilitarize Gaza in a meeting with President Trump's adviser Jared Kushner in Egypt on Sunday, according to a source with direct knowledge.

Why it matters: Kushner used the rare direct meeting to press Hamas for tangible steps on disarmament, warning that Israel doesn't trust the group to follow through.

  • The source described the 90-minute meeting as "very productive" at making sure Hamas takes practical steps to fulfill its commitments.
  • The White House and Trump's Board of Peace are pushing Hamas and Israel to move to the next phase of the U.S. 20-point peace plan.
  • Kushner is expected to visit Israel on Monday and meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss "corresponding steps" Israel must take, the source said.

Behind the scenes: Hamas leaders asked Kushner to tell Trump they remained committed to disarming, the source said.

  • "We thanked them for the commitment, but we want to see real efforts and not just words," the source added. "It was important for Kushner to lock them into this commitment in person."
  • Kushner also thanked Hamas leaders for their cooperation and efforts to recover the bodies of all deceased Israeli hostages.
  • Hamas leaders thanked the Trump administration and the Board of Peace for their efforts to improve the humanitarian situation in Gaza.

Who was there: Board of Peace high representative Nickolay Mladenov and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is also a member of the board, and Board of Peace senior advisers Aryeh Lightstone and Liran Tancman joined Kushner in the meeting.

  • Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya attended alongside Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, Qatari diplomat Ali al-Thawadi and a senior Turkish official.

Flashback: It was Kushner's first meeting with Hamas leaders since the Gaza agreement was reached last October.

Zoom in: Kushner told Hamas leaders they need to take tangible steps on disarmament if they want Israel to take steps of its own, the source said. Those steps include transferring governing authority to the Palestinian technocratic government and ensuring Hamas has no role in Gaza's future governance.

  • "Kushner stressed to Hamas leaders that the bar is high because the Israeli side doesn't trust them to actually disarm," the source said. "Kushner told them there is no room for negotiations on the disarmament, but if they show real steps the U.S. will do its best to make sure Israel takes steps of its own."
  • The board also wants Israel to conduct "corresponding steps" in Gaza if Hamas starts disarming and to accelerate humanitarian relief to the enclave.
  • "There can be no ambiguity: Hamas must relinquish governing authority and all weapons and military infrastructure. And Gaza can never again be a source of terror for Israel," the source said.

Friction point: Hamas leaders expressed frustration about Israeli policy in Gaza, including continued strikes, the source said.

  • "Kushner pushed back and said that it took them four months to agree to disarm," the source said.
  • Hamas leaders also said they are ready to hand over governance in Gaza to the Palestinian technocratic government and not interfere once it begins operating in the enclave.

What they're saying: Hamas said after the meeting that it had agreed to the roadmap for the second phase of Trump's plan, citing a permanent ceasefire, a full Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, sustained humanitarian relief and the beginning of reconstruction efforts.

  • Hamas accused Israel of failing to implement the first phase of the ceasefire agreement and called on the mediators and the Board of Peace to press Israel to meet its obligations.
  • The group also praised Trump's role in reaching the ceasefire agreement.
  • The statement did not explicitly mention disarmament.

What's next: The Board of Peace wants Hamas to begin decommissioning its weapons and military infrastructure, the source said.

  • If Hamas begins disarming, Israel's "corresponding steps" would include allowing the International Stabilization Force to deploy in Gaza, enabling reconstruction to begin in the Rafah area and discussing initial Israeli troop withdrawals, the source said.
  • The board also wants Israel to accelerate humanitarian relief to Gaza.

The big picture: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi told Kushner much of the region's instability in recent years stemmed from Gaza and that stabilizing Gaza would help the broader region, the source said.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details from Kushner's meeting with Hamas leaders, Hamas' statement after the meeting and Kushner's other meetings in Egypt.

item.title: Trump's views can factor into prosecutions, Attorney General Todd Blanche says
item.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche refused Sunday to pledge the Justice Department's independence from the White House, saying he would consider President Trump's views on individual prosecutions.

Why it matters: Trump has remade the DOJ, ousting longtime staffers, urging prosecutions of rivals and installing his former lawyer as attorney general. Blanche made the stakes clear: Trump's wishes can shape who gets investigated and prosecuted.

What he's saying: "No, I'm not going to pledge that," Blanche told NBC's "Meet the Press" after Kristen Welker asked whether DOJ would "always act independently" of the White House.

  • "And no attorney general should ever pledge that," he added.

Zoom in: Blanche said "yes, of course" Trump should have a voice in individual prosecution decisions.

  • "The president of the United States, the elected president of the United States, says something to me," he said. "And I'm supposed to say to you, 'I would say no.' I mean, that's not the way it works."

Catch up quick: Blanche called it an "extraordinarily false narrative" that Trump tells him, "Go prosecute X or Y." Yet Trump regularly broadcasts whom he wants prosecuted.

  • Last September, Trump called for prosecutions of former FBI Director James Comey, New York Attorney General Letitia James and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), writing: "They're all guilty as hell. … JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW!!!"
  • The DOJ charged Comey and James, though a judge dismissed those cases. Prosecutors later charged Comey again, over a social media post they say threatened Trump. Comey asked the judge to dismiss the case.
  • This month, Trump told D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro to revisit a vandalism case she dropped after evidence showed the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool's damage resulted from a flawed installation.

The other side: On "Fox News Sunday," Blanche told Shannon Bream that Trump "would expect me to tell him no" when they disagree legally.

  • "The president loves disagreement," he said.

Driving the news: Blanche's Sunday interviews capped his first week as attorney general after the Senate confirmed him 50–49.

  • Days after being sworn in, Blanche warmed up the crowd for Trump at a Long Island event boosting Republican candidates.
  • His nomination nearly collapsed over a Trump–IRS settlement that created a $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund.
  • Senators warned that people prosecuted for the Jan. 6 attack, including those who assaulted police, could seek payouts. GOP Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis withheld support until Blanche rescinded the order.
  • On Sunday, however, Blanche said while the fund is dead, he would not rule out Jan. 6 defendants receiving money through the government's claims process.

Context: This isn't the first time Blanche has rejected a wall between the DOJ and Trump.

  • In May, he told Congress that DOJ's policy direction comes from Trump: "We take them from the president."
  • On Steve Bannon's podcast in April, he criticized the idea that "somehow the Department of Justice is independent from the President of the United States. That is not true."
  • In written answers to Congress, he invoked the Constitution: The president is the head of the executive branch, and the Justice Department falls within that branch.

Flashback: Trump has treated alleged political influence over past attorneys general as scandalous.

  • In 2016, Trump called it disgraceful that then-Attorney General Loretta Lynch spoke privately with former President Bill Clinton on an airport tarmac.
  • Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley demanded an inspector general review of the conversation. That review found no evidence of political bias but called the meeting an error in judgment.
  • Republicans have also spent years accusing former Attorney General Merrick Garland's DOJ of political weaponization.

item.title: Scoop: Inside Trump's secret backchannel to Iran's Revolutionary Guard
item.description:
In mid-May, U.S. negotiators trying to reach a deal with Iran to end the war ran into a problem: They couldn't tell if the people across the table actually spoke for the country's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

  • So Trump administration officials did something unconventional — they went around Iran's negotiators and reached out directly to IRGC leadership. The person they tapped for the backchannel was Nechirvan Barzani, the president of the Kurdistan region in Iraq, who had something very few others do: the trust of both U.S. and IRGC leaders.

Why it matters: The episode, which was detailed by three sources with direct knowledge and has not been previously reported, shows how tricky it's been for the U.S. to negotiate with a country where Washington isn't sure who exactly is in charge. The U.S. and Iran did reach a memorandum of understanding, but it quickly collapsed.

  • The Trump administration's key problem today and in any future negotiation will be to make sure it's talking to the people who are actually calling the shots. That also means finding mediators who are trusted by both the White House and the Iranian regime.

The big picture: The war upended Iran's leadership. The assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior political leaders — and the 40 days of fighting that followed — dramatically strengthened the IRGC's grip on the levers of power, including national security and foreign policy decision-making.

  • Uncertainty surrounding new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's condition during the first few weeks of the war and his absence from public view further strengthened IRGC commanders.

Flashback: After an April 8 ceasefire and a summit in Islamabad days later, the U.S. and Iran tried to negotiate an end to the war.

  • In early May, the White House felt it was closing in on a deal, but Iran delayed its response for more than 10 days.
  • White House negotiators started to think that Iranian negotiators — Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi — were not empowered to cut a deal and were being overruled by the IRGC.

Driving the news: The White House realized it needed a backchannel to IRGC leadership.

  • Around May 10, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard called Barzani.
  • According to two sources with direct knowledge of the call, Gabbard told Barzani that the administration thought he could help get in touch with the commander of the IRGC, Gen. Ahmad Vahidi.
  • During the Iran-Iraq war, Barzani lived in Iran and studied at the University of Tehran. He is fluent in Farsi and has personal relationships with many senior members of the Iranian regime, including top members of the IRGC, according to one of the sources.
  • "Nechirvan Barzani is a pragmatic problem solver. He's respected across the region. He knows nearly everyone in Tehran as well as Washington. That's who you call in a pinch," Brett McGurk, who has served as a Middle East adviser to four presidents, said in an interview.
  • The source said Gabbard made clear to Barzani that she was making the call with the approval of President Trump and Vice President Vance.
  • Gabbard told Barzani the White House wanted to know if Vahidi and the IRGC leadership were on board with what Ghalibaf and Araghchi had been negotiating or whether they had other ideas or demands, the source said.
  • Gabbard noted the mediators couldn't reach Vahidi to clarify that.

Behind the scenes: Barzani agreed to Gabbard's request. He reached out to his contacts at the IRGC and said he had a message from the Trump administration.

  • "But I want to talk directly to Gen. Vahidi," Barzani stressed, according to one of the sources.
  • The Iranians agreed. On May 14, an IRGC official arrived in Barzani's office in Erbil, the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan, carrying an encrypted phone to conduct a secure call.
  • Barzani asked Vahidi if he was aligned with the Iranian negotiators. The Iranian general said he was. "I fully support them and this is also the position of the IRGC. We prefer to solve this crisis through negotiations," Vahidi said, according to a source with direct knowledge.
  • Three sources, including a White House official, said Barzani called Gabbard right after his conversation with Vahidi and briefed her on the Iranian response. Gabbard then briefed the White House.

The intrigue: After receiving the Iranian response, the Trump administration came back with another proposal, according to one of the sources with knowledge of the backchannel talks.

  • The U.S. wanted Barzani to host secret talks between senior U.S. and Iranian negotiators in Erbil.
  • Barzani spoke to the Iranians again and passed on the message. The Iranians didn't rule it out, but were concerned about their security, the source said.
  • They believed Israeli intelligence had many assets in Iraqi Kurdistan and were concerned the Israelis would try to assassinate them in Erbil or while they traveled there and back.
  • The Erbil meeting never materialized.

State of play: The Pakistani and Qatari mediators continue to exchange messages between the U.S. and Iran but without any significant progress, regional sources with knowledge of the matter said.

  • Some of those sources believe the Pakistanis are giving more optimistic readouts than the talks justify in an effort to create a sense of momentum that could break the stalemate.

What to watch: Barzani has recently sent messages to the White House offering to help restart U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

  • McGurk said the issue is not the mediator. "It's Iran's policy on the Strait," he said, "and that's unlikely to change anytime soon."

  • Barzani asked Vahidi if he was aligned with the Iranian negotiators. The Iranian general said he was. "I fully support them and this is also the position of the IRGC. We prefer to solve this crisis through negotiations," Vahidi said, according to a source with direct knowledge.
  • Three sources, including a White House official, said Barzani called Gabbard right after his conversation with Vahidi and briefed her on the Iranian response. Gabbard then briefed the White House.

The intrigue: After receiving the Iranian response, the Trump administration came back with another proposal, according to one of the sources with knowledge of the backchannel talks.

  • The U.S. wanted Barzani to host secret talks between senior U.S. and Iranian negotiators in Erbil.
  • Barzani spoke to the Iranians again and passed on the message. The Iranians didn't rule it out, but were concerned about their security, the source said.
  • They believed Israeli intelligence had many assets in Iraqi Kurdistan and were concerned the Israelis would try to assassinate them in Erbil or while they traveled there and back.
  • The Erbil meeting never materialized.

State of play: The Pakistani and Qatari mediators continue to exchange messages between the U.S. and Iran but without any significant progress, regional sources with knowledge of the matter said.

  • Some of those sources believe the Pakistanis are giving more optimistic readouts than the talks justify in an effort to create a sense of momentum that could break the stalemate.

What to watch: Barzani has recently sent messages to the White House offering to help restart U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

  • McGurk said the issue is not the mediator. "It's Iran's policy on the Strait," he said, "and that's unlikely to change anytime soon."

item.title: College loses its monopoly on the American Dream
item.description:
Whether framed on an office wall, collecting dust in a box or still a distant dream, the college diploma is getting a hard reappraisal.

Why it matters: College was once sold as a ticket to the American dream. But students today are taking a tougher look at the college tradeoff: burdensome debt and no guarantee of a dream career — or employment at all, as AI threatens the jobs the degrees were meant to unlock.

"People didn't ask whether college mattered 20 years ago," says Courtney Brown, the vice president of impact and planning at Lumina Foundation. Now, "they're asking: Are today's students going to be prepared for tomorrow's jobs? Is it really helping them out?"

  • Confidence in higher education slipped among both parties and all levels of educational attainment this year, according to June Gallup polling.
  • Job market fears are also surging: Gallup found just 19% of those with a college degree or more said it was a good time to find a quality job at the end of 2025, compared to 35% of those without one.

But there's a college confidence paradox: Even as Americans sour on higher education, they keep sending their kids to campus.

  • "There is still massive pressure on them from their high schools, the educators at their schools, their parents, their peers, and just the broader culture to still go to college," says The Up & Up founder and Gen Z researcher Rachel Janfaza.

The anxiety isn't new — but the reality is. Today's concerns fall into three big buckets:

  1. 💵 Affordability: "I didn't want to take out loans, and I didn't want to put my family through that stress of trying to fund it," says Gabriel Sheahan, a 24-year-old studying welding and fabrication at Lincoln Technical Institute, a trade school in New Jersey.
  2. 🏛️ Getting your money's worth: "How does it make sense that you're giving me this deadline to have my degree finished, and I can't even get the classes that I want? I'm in so much competition with all these people. It feels ... like a rat race," Rachel Sukkar, a 19-year-old philosophy major at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, says.
  3. 🎓 Outcomes: "There's just so much volatility, and you can't guarantee the same amount of success that you could 20 years ago with a college degree now," says Moksha Agrawal, a 17-year-old incoming high school senior.

Zoom out: Vocational and trade programs provide an alternative route.

  • Sheahan notes that welding is hard work, but he's already completed key industry certifications and can picture a clear, stable career path.
  • "The trades have been so demonized over the last 30 years that everybody wants to either now be a TikTok star, an influencer, a Jeff Bezos," he says. Still, "there's such a high percentage of kids that get out of college and whatever degree they have ... they never will work in it."

The bottom line: High schools and colleges need to adapt to the changing job market, Janfaza says, giving more weight to extracurriculars and soft skills.

  • And just like the savvy shopper reads reviews, students need to see real results from institutions to prove their worth.
  • "It's not a marketing campaign — I'm not saying go make another billboard," Brown tells Axios. "But show it really in the outcomes of your students."
