item.title: Trump's White House remodel tab keeps growing
item.description:
The East Wing is gone, a new helipad is spreading across the lawn, and scaffolding wraps the White House's front columns, but the price tags for President Trump's renovations are far less obvious.

The big picture: The muddled mix of funding streams — whether from private donors, the president himself or taxpayers — has fueled ethical questions about who's footing the ever-rising bill for the HGTV-reminiscent White House redesign.

The latest: Senate Democrats urged the Government Accountability Office to audit the ballroom project's scope and cost Wednesday.

  • One tally, reported exclusively by The Washington Post this week, says the president's construction projects, including upgrades to Lafayette Square and other renovations, could cost at least $927 million.
  • The lawmakers cited a lack of transparency and "limited congressional oversight, meaningful public input, and adherence to established federal processes."

What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that Trump "continues to implement long-overdue and necessary renovations," calling him the "Builder-in-Chief."

  • As the administration has argued in court, Ingle said the East Wing project is "inextricably tied" to security concerns, pointing to an alleged plot to attack this summer's UFC fight on White House grounds.
  • A senior administration official said the ballroom would be built with private donations, not tax dollars. Reported donors include Google, Apple, Amazon and Lockheed Martin, among several other household names.

Zoom in: While critics demand more specifics on the costs and sources of funding, one thing is clear: 18 months in, Trump's construction itch hasn't eased, and the price tag keeps on growing with it.

Zoom out: While the East Wing's demolition might be the most head-turning change, an unclear cascade of cash is being poured into other projects, as well, including:

  • A helipad for the new Marine One model, with Lockheed Martin covering up to $6 million.
  • The Rose Garden re-do, which reportedly cost around $2 million, covered by private donations.
  • A granite pathway to the Oval Office that Trump said he was paying for — though an investigation by The Atlantic said otherwise.

Zoom in: The stalled ballroom project's price tag has risen rapidly after it was initially pitched at roughly $200 million last year.

  • Trump then told reporters earlier this year the cost could be between $300 million or $400 million, "depending on finishes," like "very expensive marble."
  • He defended the price hike in May, writing on Truth Social the estimate doubled because "it is approximately twice the size, and a far higher quality, than the original proposal."
  • The Washington Post, citing a summary compiled by the contractor behind the project, reported the estimated cost was closer to $600 million in June — and that taxpayer dollars were being funneled to the project.

Catch up quick: Above-ground construction of the ballroom has been blocked by judges, who say Trump needs congressional approval to proceed.

Friction point: The administration also pitched lawmakers on a $1 billion security plan for the renovation project, Axios' Alex Isenstadt previously reported, including $220 million for "hardening" security and $180 million for a new visitor screening facility.

  • Republicans didn't bite — and the funding has continued to be a source of scrutiny on the Hill.
  • In June, Democrats raised questions about why One Big Beautiful Bill funds for the Secret Service were directed to White House security.

Worth noting: Trump's smaller redecorating touches are also indicative of his approach to his temporary home.

  • He's erected a wall of plaques honoring some former presidents — and mocking others. The Oval Office has gradually grown more gilded and the artwork has changed.
  • Plus, he's not stopping on Penn. Ave.

Go deeper: Haberman: 70% of Trump's brain on monuments

item.title: Maggie Haberman says 70% of Trump's attention goes to monuments, renovations and legacy
item.description:
The New York Times' Maggie Haberman tells me 70% of President Trump's mindshare ("maybe plus or minus 5%") goes to his gilding, construction, renovation, renaming and tribute projects.

  • "He is spending a huge amount of energy, mental and otherwise, on these renovation projects, beautification projects around Washington, and then monuments to self," Haberman told me for Axios' "Behind the Curtain" video series. "[T]here is no precedent in U.S. history of a sitting president devising such endeavors in their own name."

Why it matters: That mental map by Haberman — co-author with Jonathan Swan of "Regime Change," which has sold 600,000 copies and on Wednesday hit seven weeks at No. 1 on the New York Times bestseller list — is a Rosetta Stone to what motivates and fascinates Trump.

  • "What interests him are things that you can see and touch," she told Axios.

The backstory: Haberman had earlier made the 70% estimate about Trump's mindshare during an interview with her Times colleague Ezra Klein, saying that it's "a legacy thing."

  • Maggie and I worked together in the early years of Politico. Her relentless reporting has made the New York City native a top expert on how Trump thinks. So I asked her to unpack her eye-opening stat:

Zoom in: Haberman and Swan visited Trump in the Oval Office in March for an hourlong interview for the book, which is now in eight printings and is the nonfiction bestseller of the year.

  • "It was very clear," Haberman recalled, "what his mind was on while we were there. And what it was not really on was the war," which he'd launched just over two weeks earlier.
  • "He didn't really want to talk about that. He didn't really want to talk about policy specifics. He wanted to describe himself as winning. And he wanted to show us how he had remade Washington."

Behind the scenes: "You would think that on the 17th day of the war that he would have maps of the Middle East or maps of troop deployments — who knows," Haberman continued. "He picks up these pictures, and [they're] of maple trees. And he says: 'I am choosing maple trees for the White House. I am good at picking trees.' I'm paraphrasing here, but that is pretty much what he said."

  • "Under that were designs of the ballroom. And he starts talking to us about the columns and how some of the columns are evocative of Rome. And then on the other side, the columns are evocative of Athens. And he's happy that they are a little bit either wider or more spaced apart or both than the columns at the Supreme Court. And that was like the first 15 minutes of this hour that we had."

Go deeper: Share the video.

item.title: Musk and Zuckerberg claw back into AI race with new model momentum
item.description:
Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg have muscled their way back into AI's elite ranks, defying early obituaries to close the gap on a new generation of Silicon Valley startups.

Why it matters: Recent gains by tech giants SpaceX and Meta — long stuck in AI's second tier — are putting new pressure on a hierarchy dominated by OpenAI and Anthropic.

State of play: Both companies released models this week featuring a combination of performance and price that would have been hard to imagine from either lab a year ago.

  • SpaceX's Grok 4.6 scored essentially even with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol Max on the closely watched Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and just behind Anthropic's Fable 5 Max.
  • Promising "something special," Musk said Grok 4.7 should arrive in three to four weeks and predicted it will "exceed all current models" after additional training on a massive trove of SpaceX data.

Meta, meanwhile, is trying to squeeze the frontier from below.

  • Its new models deliver competitive performance at dramatically lower cost — including Muse Glimmer, an open-weight system small enough to run locally on a laptop.
  • Zuckerberg cast the push as "superintelligence for everyone" in a sweeping manifesto this week, reviving Meta's open-AI ambitions as the U.S. races to regain ground from China.

Catch up quick: As OpenAI and Anthropic pulled ahead, Musk and Zuckerberg answered with the full force of their empires — spending billions on talent, infrastructure and acquisitions.

  • Zuckerberg overhauled Meta's AI effort after the disappointing launch of Llama 4, then invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI and brought aboard its CEO, Alexandr Wang, to lead the push.
  • Musk went even further, folding xAI into SpaceX and agreeing to acquire Cursor for $60 billion — bringing massive computing power, proprietary SpaceX data and a fast-growing AI coding platform under one roof.

Between the lines: The AI race is starting to reward more than raw intelligence, as price becomes a decisive advantage for many users.

  • "You don't need to be the highest-performing, most expensive model in the market to be able to be successful," Sonali Basak, chief investment strategist at iCapital, told Axios.
  • Basak said that raises a more consequential question for Musk and Zuckerberg: whether their AI advancements can "fuel the core businesses" that financed their comeback.

Reality check: The frontier labs still hold pole position — with even more capable models waiting in the wings, including systems deemed too sensitive for public release.

  • "I wouldn't say they've caught up to OpenAI or Anthropic," said John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds.
  • A Meta employee told Axios the company still feels behind the frontier labs in model performance and development.

What we're watching: Turbulence at Google could create an opening for either company to seize its place as Wall Street's public-market AI champion.

  • Google had emerged as the established tech giant best positioned to challenge OpenAI and Anthropic, pairing elite talent with enormous resources and early momentum.
  • That position suddenly looks shakier after an exodus of top AI talent — including Google's chief scientist — and setbacks involving its flagship model Gemini.

The bottom line: OpenAI and Anthropic built their lead through years of technical excellence. Musk and Zuckerberg are nipping at their heels with decades of scale and resources.

Meta, meanwhile, is trying to squeeze the frontier from below.

  • Its new models deliver competitive performance at dramatically lower cost — including Muse Glimmer, an open-weight system small enough to run locally on a laptop.
  • Zuckerberg cast the push as "superintelligence for everyone" in a sweeping manifesto this week, reviving Meta's open-AI ambitions as the U.S. races to regain ground from China.

Catch up quick: As OpenAI and Anthropic pulled ahead, Musk and Zuckerberg answered with the full force of their empires — spending billions on talent, infrastructure and acquisitions.

  • Zuckerberg overhauled Meta's AI effort after the disappointing launch of Llama 4, then invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI and brought aboard its CEO, Alexandr Wang, to lead the push.
  • Musk went even further, folding xAI into SpaceX and agreeing to acquire Cursor for $60 billion — bringing massive computing power, proprietary SpaceX data and a fast-growing AI coding platform under one roof.

Between the lines: The AI race is starting to reward more than raw intelligence, as price becomes a decisive advantage for many users.

  • "You don't need to be the highest-performing, most expensive model in the market to be able to be successful," Sonali Basak, chief investment strategist at iCapital, told Axios.
  • Basak said that raises a more consequential question for Musk and Zuckerberg: whether their AI advancements can "fuel the core businesses" that financed their comeback.

Reality check: The frontier labs still hold pole position — with even more capable models waiting in the wings, including systems deemed too sensitive for public release.

  • "I wouldn't say they've caught up to OpenAI or Anthropic," said John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds.
  • A Meta employee told Axios the company still feels behind the frontier labs in model performance and development.

What we're watching: Turbulence at Google could create an opening for either company to seize its place as Wall Street's public-market AI champion.

  • Google had emerged as the established tech giant best positioned to challenge OpenAI and Anthropic, pairing elite talent with enormous resources and early momentum.
  • That position suddenly looks shakier after an exodus of top AI talent — including Google's chief scientist — and setbacks involving its flagship model Gemini.

The bottom line: OpenAI and Anthropic built their lead through years of technical excellence. Musk and Zuckerberg are nipping at their heels with decades of scale and resources.

item.title: Pollsters missed again in Wisconsin. Here's why.
item.description:
Pollsters appeared to blow another high-stakes Midwest election Tuesday, as center-left Democrat David Crowley stunned socialist Francesca Hong in Wisconsin's primary for governor.

  • But on Wednesday, the reasons for the miss seemed clear: Surveys a week before the primary captured only a hint of a rapidly changing roller coaster of a race in which Crowley was gaining fast, and Hong was playing defense.

Driving the news: Two polls had shown Hong up by about 20 points over Crowley. But Crowley wound up winning by half a percentage point in an upset that interrupted a run of primary wins by left-wing Democrats this spring.

  • Just a week earlier, polls also had overestimated progressive Abdul El-Sayed's strength in the Michigan Senate race by double digits. He won by 1 point.

Polls help shape the pre-election narrative for campaigns, but the Midwest misses were reminders of the surveys' limitations in capturing voters' feelings over just a few days in a long race.

  • In the days before the primary, even Crowley's own pollster had him down by nearly 20 points.

Zoom in: The final month of the gubernatorial primary was particularly chaotic. There was a mad dash by the party's establishment to stop Hong out of fear that the state Assembly member was too far left to win in November.

  • Two candidates dropped out amid sudden scandals. Crowley, the county executive in Milwaukee, actually exited his campaign as well — then re-entered the race to try to take out Hong.
  • The last week of the campaign was dominated by the fallout from Hong struggling to explain to CNN why she'd once taken to social media to say "cancel Thanksgiving."

Amid that hurricane, Democratic strategists saw late-deciding voters flocking toward Crowley as he barnstormed Wisconsin with Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, questioning Hong's electability.

  • Even some people at Hong's events said they were undecided as the primary approached.
  • "Part of it is the old saw that we often say but rarely hear: Polling is a snapshot in time," former top Obama strategist David Axelrod told us. "A lot of the polls were taken too early to capture the movement."

Just dig into the numbers. Hong won about 39% of the electorate — and the final polls had her in the low 40s.

  • It was Crowley whose standing appeared to change dramatically — jumping from around 20% support to roughly 40% within days.
  • Another factor that helps explain the miss, strategists told us, is that it's difficult for pollsters to model an open primary, in which voters can participate in either party's primary regardless of their registration.
  • "It's hard to know who's going to show up," Axelrod said.

The intrigue: Chaz Nuttycombe, founder of the nonpartisan group State Navigate, put out one of the early August polls that had Hong up by double digits.

  • He speculated that in Wisconsin's open primary, some people who usually vote in Republican primaries may have crossed over to vote in the more competitive Democratic contest to stop Hong.
  • Fox was airing wall-to-wall coverage about Hong at the time.
  • Nuttycombe also said his site's last poll received more than 10,000 visits from IP addresses in Wisconsin and the surrounding area — an indication that many anti-Hong voters were paying close attention to polling in the race last weekend and likely used it to determine which alternative candidate they should support.

Dan Pfeiffer, another former top adviser to President Obama, noted on X and Substack that Hong — with little campaign money — also didn't air TV ads during the campaign's stretch run to counter the attacks against her in the critical last few days before the primary.

  • "Hong ran an inspirational grassroots campaign that mobilized people around key issues like data centers, but her failure to advertise in the final days probably cost her the election," Pfeiffer wrote.
  • "In the final days, voters only heard concerns about Hong, but no countervailing positive message."

item.title: Youth poll: Thumbs down on everything
item.description:
Data: Generation Lab; Chart: Danielle Alberti/Axios

More than a quarter of younger Americans (27%) believe they or someone they know has lost a job because their employer replaced them with AI, according to a new Axios-Generation Lab poll of 18- to 34-year-olds.

Why it matters: Research suggests the actual share of job losses from AI is smaller. But the survey reflects the suspicion, mistrust and fatalism in how Gen Zers and young Millennials see the technology — sentiments driving their views on politics, the economy and social interactions.

  • Asked which political party they trust more to bring down the cost of living, respondents' top choice was neither (36%) — over Democrats (26%) and Republicans (22%).

What they're saying: "They're kind of thumbs-down on everything — how the president's doing, how the economy's doing, both political parties," said Generation Lab CEO Cyrus Beschloss. "AI is a pretty big disruptor; it's easy to point to one faceless thing as the cause."

  • Despite fears of AI stealing jobs, 71% said they're as comfortable or more comfortable with it than they were a year ago; 61% said they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48% reported using Gemini and 20% Claude.

What we're watching: 96% are concerned about the cost of rent, groceries, gas or utilities, including 40% who are "extremely" concerned.

  • 48% rate the national economy as "poor."
  • 35% said if they were looking for a job today it would be "very difficult." Another 43% said it would be "somewhat difficult."
  • More than half say home ownership is a top goal. But only about half think they'll own a home in the next decade, and 28% say it's very unlikely.

By the numbers: 66% disapprove of President Trump's handling of his job, 54% strongly.

  • 64% disapprove of Trump's handling of the war with Iran, 50% strongly. Two-thirds believe the war has left the U.S. worse off than before.

Looking ahead to 2028 presidential election, name recognition appears to be a significant factor.

  • Among Democratic respondents, former Vice President Kamala Harris led a field of prospective presidential candidates (28.7%), followed by former First Lady Michelle Obama (14.9%) and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (11.7%).
  • Independents favored Michelle Obama (11.4%), AOC (9.2%) and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders (7.4%).
  • Among Republican respondents, Vice President JD Vance was the clear leader (31.5%), followed by the president's son Donald Trump Jr. (10.7%) and Secretary of State Marco Rubio (9.7%).

Zoom in: Last November, an Axios-Generation Lab poll found that 67% of two- and four-year college students had a positive or neutral association with the word "socialism" compared with just 40% with a positive or neutral view of "capitalism." We wrote then that this reflected college students' left lean as well as economic conditions.

  • But this latest poll captures the broader sentiments of Americans under 35, including some long done with college and others with only high school degrees or no diploma — and the results weren't that different.
  • 68% of respondents say they view socialism positively or neutrally, while 47% have positive or neutral views of capitalism. Negative views of capitalism outweigh negative views of socialism by more than 2 to 1.

"I don't think it's young people sitting around thinking about what economic models are most beneficial to society at large, or reading Plato's Republic and pondering economic theory," Beschloss said.

  • "They may be thinking it's a radical way to shake things up, shake up the status quo — a way to give things to the working class, an anti-establishment thing, more than the clear workings of socialism."

Methodology: This poll was conducted July 29-Aug. 4, 2026, from a representative sample of 1,075 adults ages 18-34, including 244 with high school degrees or less, 457 with some college or an associate's degree and 374 with bachelor's degrees or higher.

  • 37% of respondents identified as Democrats, 26% as Republicans and 29% as independents.
  • The overall margin of error is +/- 3.01 percentage points.

item.title: Why House Dems may go easy on one of GOP's most vulnerable members
item.description:
Rep. Mike Lawler's (R-N.Y.) fight to hold on to a key battleground seat is getting a behind-the-scenes assist — for now, at least — from an unlikely group: House Democrats.

Why it matters: Kamala Harris carried Lawler's district in 2024, but some Democrats are privately wary of spending the small fortune it would take to oust one of the GOP's most bipartisan — and electorally savvy — members.

  • "If you're going to have a Republican, it's the kind of Republican we want in the Congress," a Democratic source told Axios of Lawler, also noting that the New York City area is the nation's most expensive media market.
  • A senior House Democrat told Axios: "I don't think Lawler is beatable."

State of play: Republicans are outspending Democrats more than 40 to 1 on current and future ad reservations in New York's 17th District, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact.

  • The House Republican leadership–aligned super PAC Congressional Leadership Fund has a whopping $6.7 million reserved in the district.
  • That is on top of $2.8 million from the Lawler campaign and $2.1 million from outside GOP group Americans for Open Government.
  • Democratic leadership–aligned nonprofit House Majority Forward is the only group with ad reservations in the district, at just $270,000 reserved.

Yes, but: Democrats insist their lack of ad reservations is simply a result of the New York media market being so costly that there is no value in reserving TV time early there compared with states like Iowa.

  • "NY-17 is one of the best flip opportunities on the map, and Mike Lawler is down in polling — HMP is going to do whatever it takes to flip this seat," CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for the HMF's political arm, House Majority PAC, told Axios.
  • Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Riya Vashi pointed to an alleged GOP shell PAC spending $1.5 million in a failed attempt to stop Cait Conley from becoming the Democratic nominee as evidence they are "clearly scared."
  • Vashi noted that the DCCC put Conley, a U.S. Army veteran, on its coveted "Red to Blue" list and said the group will "continue our efforts to fire Mike Lawler and elect Cait every day leading up to November."

Zoom out: Lawler's Hudson Valley district has long been viewed as one of Democrats' best pickup opportunities — and one of the races most likely to decide control of the House.

  • Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to reclaim the majority.
  • Harris carried Lawler's district by half a percentage point in 2024, making it the most Democratic-leaning seat in which a House Republican is running for reelection.

Between the lines: One estimate shared with Axios found that the money needed to compete seriously in NY-17 could instead fund television advertising across 11 toss-up House districts.

  • The only other truly vulnerable GOP incumbent in the NYC media market besides Lawler is Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-N.J.), and Democrats wouldn't get much bang for their buck spending there.
  • Said the Democratic source: "If you can pick up five people for the cost of one person, wouldn't you just go after the five people?"

The intrigue: A former House Republican familiar with the dynamic between Lawler and Democratic leadership expressed skepticism that Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) will ultimately lay off Lawler through Election Day.

  • The tensions between Lawler and Jeffries spilled into the open last year when Lawler waited outside the Democratic leader's press conference and the two engaged in a shouting match over the ongoing government shutdown.
  • The DCCC and House Majority PAC will "absolutely" spend in the district because "Schumer and Jeffries hate him," the former lawmaker predicted, adding that Lawler "will still win."
  • A second senior House Democrat, asked if Jeffries hates Lawler, told Axios: "Correct."

The bottom line: Lawler is one of the Republicans with the most Democratic fans, but he's still a Republican standing between them and the House majority.

item.title: Congressional campaign stars
item.description:
It's August, which means lawmakers are fanning out across the country to campaign for themselves and their colleagues.

Why it matters: A friendly senator or House member can help on the stump. But only a handful can juice fundraising, draw a real crowd or make a mark with an endorsement. And Democrats have more of them.

Zoom in: Axios asked strategists in both parties which lawmakers have enough star power to move voters, draw crowds or open wallets for candidates far from home.

  • There aren't many, but a few names came up again and again.

For Democrats: No one compares to former President Obama. But among lawmakers, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has never been hotter, as progressives and democratic socialists take down one establishment-backed candidate after another.

  • In a twist, Sanders is seen by some Democrats as an asset not just in the primary — but also in the upcoming general election.
  • Sanders appeared in one of battleground House candidate Rebecca Cooke's closing primary ads in this week's Wisconsin primary. Her other final ad pitched a Sanders idea — a moratorium on data centers.
  • "Public and private polls show that a lot of the working people Democrats have to win back respect Bernie Sanders because they want candid, populist leaders with the backbone to fight an economic status quo that has failed them," Democratic strategist and former Biden spokesperson Andrew Bates, who advises Cooke, told Axios.
  • "He's also an opponent of out-of-touch ideas that turn swing voters away, like 'defunding the police,'" Bates continued.

Sanders' heir-apparent, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), also tops the list with her formidable grassroots power.

  • Sanders and AOC combined have drawn huge crowds across the country, even when they're not explicitly campaigning for themselves.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) is also popular nationwide, bolstered by his experience as an astronaut.

👀 Both Kelly and AOC are potential 2028 presidential election contenders.

  • And few endorsements are seen as carrying more weight with Black voters than that of Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.).
  • (That said, Clyburn's preferred candidate in the Michigan Senate primary just lost despite his campaigning for her. He also endorsed failed New York City mayoral candidate Andrew Cuomo in 2025.)
  • Former presidential candidates like Sen. Cory Booker (N.J.). and Elizabeth Warren (D- Mass.) are still big names on the trail, but their presence is not as potent as it once was.

For Republicans: The roster of lawmakers outside of leadership is shorter. And, of course, no member of Congress comes close to matching the power of President Trump and some in his Cabinet.

  • Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) has become an online and in-person phenomenon with his folksy one-liners and viral clips.
  • "When I go into a state and headline a fundraiser for one of my colleagues, it seems to attract people," Kennedy told Politico's Jordain Carney. "I think I'm like the new animal in the zoo."

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) is polarizing but familiar, with the ability to draw crowds and Texas dollars.

  • Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), as a founder of the House Freedom Caucus, can do a lot for a candidate.

Between the lines: Power in Washington doesn't necessarily translate to power on the campaign trail. Although Hill leaders' job is to work to keep their majorities, they still hold the most sway with major donors, not average voters.

  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) are bringing in record funds — even as roughly a third of voters say they have never heard of Thune and 44% disapprove of Schumer, according to a recent CNN poll.
  • Thune even told reporters last month that his endorsement "probably isn't helpful anyway" when asked about South Carolina Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) often gets media coverage of his cross-country efforts to campaign for House Republican candidates, as does his leadership team — Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Tom Emmer (R-Minn.)

  • 30% of voters said they had never heard of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, even as he campaigned recently for Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and battleground House candidate Bob Brooks.

  • (That said, Clyburn's preferred candidate in the Michigan Senate primary just lost despite his campaigning for her. He also endorsed failed New York City mayoral candidate Andrew Cuomo in 2025.)
  • Former presidential candidates like Sen. Cory Booker (N.J.). and Elizabeth Warren (D- Mass.) are still big names on the trail, but their presence is not as potent as it once was.

For Republicans: The roster of lawmakers outside of leadership is shorter. And, of course, no member of Congress comes close to matching the power of President Trump and some in his Cabinet.

  • Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) has become an online and in-person phenomenon with his folksy one-liners and viral clips.
  • "When I go into a state and headline a fundraiser for one of my colleagues, it seems to attract people," Kennedy told Politico's Jordain Carney. "I think I'm like the new animal in the zoo."

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) is polarizing but familiar, with the ability to draw crowds and Texas dollars.

  • Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), as a founder of the House Freedom Caucus, can do a lot for a candidate.

Between the lines: Power in Washington doesn't necessarily translate to power on the campaign trail. Although Hill leaders' job is to work to keep their majorities, they still hold the most sway with major donors, not average voters.

  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) are bringing in record funds — even as roughly a third of voters say they have never heard of Thune and 44% disapprove of Schumer, according to a recent CNN poll.
  • Thune even told reporters last month that his endorsement "probably isn't helpful anyway" when asked about South Carolina Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) often gets media coverage of his cross-country efforts to campaign for House Republican candidates, as does his leadership team — Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Tom Emmer (R-Minn.)

  • 30% of voters said they had never heard of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, even as he campaigned recently for Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and battleground House candidate Bob Brooks.

item.title: Karoline Leavitt stepping down as White House press secretary
item.description:
Karoline Leavitt will be stepping down from her role as White House press secretary at the end of the month, President Trump announced Wednesday in a Truth Social post.

The big picture: Leavitt is leaving to spend more time with her family, the president said. A member of Trump's team who followed him from his presidential campaign to the White House, she's been a fiercely loyal face of the White House.

Driving the news: Trump said in the surprise post that Leavitt will become one of his top outside advisers and "an influential voice within the Republican Party" heading into the midterm elections.

  • Leavitt, 28, said in a post that being a mother and welcoming a new baby while serving as press secretary "has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least."
  • She continued, "The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary."
  • When reached for comment, the White House pointed to statements made by Leavitt and Trump.

Zoom in: Leavitt made headlines for being the youngest White House press secretary to hold the role.

  • She defended the White House through multiple controversies and the biggest stories of the president's second term so far, including the Signalgate scandal, the release of the Epstein files and the Iran war.
  • Even in her statement announcing her departure, she took aim at Democrats that she said seek "to destroy everything great about America."
  • Leavitt also backed the Trump administration's tightening of press coverage, telling Axios last year that the administration wanted to expand access — opening the press corps to influencers and MAGA-friendly voices — and not limit it.

Context: The president directly chooses the White House press secretary, a position that does not require Senate confirmation.

  • Trump had four press secretaries during his first term.

Editor's note: This story was updated throughout with additional information.

item.title: Trump's ballroom costs are rising. What we know about the secret underground bunker
item.description:
The development costs of President Trump's White House ballroom keep rising — as does speculation about what the finished project, including its underground complex, will look like.

The big picture: Trump's ballroom project is more than a simple remodel of the East Wing. It's a complete overhaul featuring what appears to be a military-grade underground bunker, meant to protect and secure the president.

  • The project remains in legal limbo after a federal appeals court ruled in August that Trump's ballroom plans need congressional approval. Trump said he plans to ask the Supreme Court to overturn the decision.

By the numbers: The ballroom is expected to cost around $600 million — with about half of that coming from taxpayer dollars, The Washington Post reported.

  • It's an increase from the White House's initial $200 million estimate, which they said would come from private donors. That amount was later amended to $400 million and then $600 million.

Trump's administration is also planning to spend at least an additional $300 million on other projects around the White House complex, including a helipad, a visitor screening center and changes to the Rose Garden, the Post reported.

  • In May, the Trump administration reportedly suggested asking taxpayers for $1 billion for security upgrades across the entire White House campus, though lawmakers seemed unconvinced by the request.

Reality check: Specifics about the ballroom and its underground complex remain unclear, as many of the details remain classified.

  • Trump himself has pointed to the "massive complex" being built underneath the ballroom.

Read what we know below.

What we know about the underground bunker

Architect Shalom Baranes presents plans for President Trump's proposed White House ballroom to the National Capital Planning Commission in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 8. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Zoom out: The size of the underground aspect of the projects lacks clarity, though the National Capital Planning Commission's official plan suggests it ranges around 22,000 square feet.

  • "The military is building a massive complex under the ballroom, and that's under construction, and we're doing very well," Trump said in April.
  • Trump said the complex goes six stories deep and that the ballroom itself features a "drone-proof" roof and a "drone port."
  • He also said the bunker will have bomb shelters and medical facilities.

The underground complex mostly aims to modify and potentially replace the Presidential Emergency Operations Center (PEOC), which is a secure underground bunker built during World War II that has been updated over decades.

  • The PEOC has been used for short-term shelter for officials. It was used to protect Vice President Dick Cheney and National Security Adviser Condoleezza Rice during the September 11 attacks.
  • Trump was protected there too during 2020 protests following the death of George Floyd, per the New York Times.

What the entire ballroom project has

Construction continues on President Trump's White House ballroom and a new South Lawn helipad in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 10. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The entire ballroom project includes features that aim to protect the president.

  • Specifics about the ballroom project have been spelled out in a lawsuit filed by the National Trust for Historic Preservation against the project's construction.
  • The entire facility has "military-grade" vents for air conditioning, hospital and medical facilities, "top secret "military installations, and "bomb shelters," the filing says.

The massive complex has been described in lawsuits as a national security facility.

  • The project includes "bunkers, bomb-shelters, and military and medical infrastructure," per the D.C. Circuit.
  • Government officials have described the security features as necessary to defend the president from drones, missiles and biohazards, per AP.

Why the White House wants the renovations

What they're saying: "The East Wing Modernization Project is inextricably tied to the security of the President, the White House grounds and the certain security infrastructure assets," Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, tells Axios.

  • The White House has pointed to the foiled attack plot planned for the White House's UFC fight in July and the White House Correspondents Dinner attack as reasons to add security upgrades.

Zoom out: Matthew Quinn, deputy director of the Secret Service, wrote in a court filing in April that the ballroom will help keep the president safe.

  • "An above-ground slab and topping structure is needed to ensure that key underground structures with a security purpose are properly protected and strengthened," he wrote.
  • "Leaving the project site unfinished imperils the ability of the Secret Service to meet its statutory mission to protect the President."

Go deeper: White House makeover under Trump: See all the proposed changes

Avery Lotz contributed to this report.

item.title: ICE plans to put electric-shock gloves on officers' hands
item.description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to begin using electric shock gloves designed to cause pain and disrupt a person's ability to react.

The big picture: The gloves could give ICE officers a new way to use force as their tactics face intense scrutiny after several deaths and violent encounters.

Driving the news: ICE plans to spend between $10 and $20 million on the gloves and issue them to Homeland Security Investigations and Enforcement Removal Operations officers and agents, per a Department of Homeland Security notice published Monday.

  • The Associated Press was first to report the plan.
  • The CTG-5 Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, or G.L.O.V.E, is produced by Kentucky-based Compliant Technologies, which declined to comment.
  • The device's user guide says it should not be used against verbal defiance or as a form of punishment. The manufacturer advises against using it on the elderly, children, pregnant women and those with serious disabilities.

Friction point: Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, ACLU's deputy director on policing, raised concerns about how immigration agents could use the device.

  • "ICE spent the last year showing this country that they are willing to disregard the law and are too quick to use force, with devastating and at times fatal consequences for citizens and noncitizens alike," she said in a statement.
  • She noted officers could use the gloves to deliver shocks covertly, "a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability."

The fine print: The gloves are meant to stop detainees or subjects from "performing coordinated muscle movement" by causing pain through direct skin contact.

  • G.L.O.V.E. users must undergo training for certification every two years, according to the manufacturer's user manual.
  • A DHS spokesperson said in a statement that officers are "highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training."

Worth noting: ICE is also expanding its use of body cameras after the agency's fatal shootings and other use-of-force incidents.

Zoom out: In the background, millions of people are living in immigration limbo — colliding with the reality of ramped-up enforcement at airports, application interviews and beyond, Axios' Brittany Gibson reports.

  • ICE has been infused with billions from Republican lawmakers as the administration maintains lofty goals to remove unauthorized immigrants from the U.S.

Go deeper: Trump deportations cost taxpayers $2,358 each

item.title: Quantifying the AI boom crowding-out effect
item.description:
When investment on the scale of the current AI boom occurs, it inevitably has to come at the expense of something. All the resources devoted to building data centers and developing AI models would otherwise go to something else.

The big picture: This crowding out is smaller than you might expect, Goldman Sachs economists find in a new note.

  • But it does exist, they say, and takes the form of displacing other tech investment and construction, as well as raising corporate borrowing costs.

By the numbers: AI investment will be about $600 billion this year, some 2% of GDP, accounting for 10% of business fixed investment and 15% of equipment investment, economists Jessica Rindels and David Mericle wrote.

State of play: The first crowding-out channel they identify is the displacement of other tech spending at the hyperscalers themselves and at the companies that spend cold, hard cash on AI services.

  • Corporate IT budgets, for example, that face new, big costs for AI tokens may seek to cut back on other software and tech spending.
  • That doesn't have much impact on overall GDP, however, as it amounts to shifting spending around.

Zoom out: The Goldman team also sees the data center boom crowding out other building activity, as construction labor and equipment is devoted to the AI buildout.

  • Gross margins on data center construction are more than twice as high as margins on non-tech projects, Rindels and Mericle wrote, "which has resulted in data centers pulling resources away from other projects."

Zoom in: The hyperscalers' bottomless demand for capital has created a surge in AI-related debt issuance. The rest of the corporate sector faces higher borrowing costs as a result — which may hem in their own investment.

  • But the Goldman team finds that this impact has been limited so far, raising corporate borrowing costs by only 0.05 percentage point and perhaps reducing non-AI investment by a modest $10 billion.

The bottom line: "While media reports and market commentary often claim that AI is making a very large contribution to U.S. GDP growth but also crowding out a great deal of other activity," Rindels and Mericle wrote, their analysis "suggests that both claims are exaggerated."

item.title: Diesel desperation is mounting globally
item.description:
The state of the global diesel market is getting even more precarious as the Russia-Ukraine war and the Iran crisis squeeze supply from multiple angles.

Why it matters: Diesel prices ripple through economies here and abroad, affecting shipping costs, construction and plenty in between.

  • The average U.S. price is up 44 cents over the last month to $5.32 per gallon, compared to $3.71 a year ago, per AAA.
  • However, during the Iran crisis, it hasn't hit the all-time high of $5.82 per gallon that AAA recorded in mid-June of 2022.

Driving the news: A new S&P Global Energy analysis unpacks the ingredients behind the "big squeeze" in global refined product markets.

  • S&P estimates that refineries worldwide processed 7.5 million barrels per day less crude last month than the same period in 2025.
  • A separate International Energy Agency analysis out this morning also tracks an extremely steep drop in how much crude that refineries are processing.
Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

State of play: Renewed hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz are further restricting supply after a period of optimism about normalizing flows.

  • Middle East refineries are processing much less as capacity remains "physically impaired, logistically stranded, or operationally unable to restart with confidence," S&P states.
  • Russia's restrictions on diesel exports following Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries have removed another 10% of seaborne supplies from the market, and China's refinery activity remains "subdued."

By the numbers: Diesel exports from Russia, the Middle East and Asia in July were 1.3 million barrels per day lower year-over-year, "equivalent to about 20% of global seaborne trade," IEA's monthly report this morning states.

"Diesel is the tightest market right now," Amrita Sen, founder of market intelligence firm Energy Aspects, tells Bloomberg TV.

Zoom in: In the U.S., the Energy Department's stats and analysis arm yesterday revised its diesel price estimates upward.

  • The Energy Information Administration sees retail prices averaging $4.85 per gallon in 2026, compared to $4.61 in last month's outlook.
  • It also slightly raised its 2027 forecast average to $4.07, up from $4.02.

The big picture: In the U.S., fuel accounts for roughly 20-25% of trucking companies' operating costs, according to the American Trucking Associations, a major trade group.

What we're watching: The U.S. has been exporting growing amounts of diesel to the thirsty global market, but S&P points out that U.S. refineries are running at 96% of capacity.

  • With the heart of hurricane season and traditional fall maintenance looming, the market's remaining buffers are very thin, the research and consulting firm notes.
  • And diesel and similar refinery products are used for heating in many countries. "I think we are underestimating just how tight diesel can be this winter," said Sen.

The bottom line: "The situation is not going away anytime soon and could very well get more expensive," Mizuho Securities analyst Robert Yawger said in a note.

  • "Ukrainian drone production has been increasing exponentially, with Russian energy infrastructure a prime target," he writes.
  • "Unless there are big breakthroughs in the peace process around both conflicts, large amounts of diesel will remain shut in."

item.title: Socialist fever breaks: Takeaways from Crowley's win
item.description:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly defeated socialist Francesca Hong by about 3,000 votes, dealing a blow to the progressive left's momentum Tuesday in Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, after his own polling indicated he was behind by nearly 20 points.

Why it matters: Crowley's win could breathe new life into a center-left that had been losing primary after primary in recent months, from last week's Senate contest in Michigan to House races across the country.

Yes, but: The day wasn't a total loss for progressives.

  • In the day's other big ideological showdown between Democrats, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive, defeated moderate Rep. Angie Craig in Minnesota's Senate primary by 20 points.
  • Flanagan will face GOP nominee Michele Tafoya, a former NFL TV reporter, in November.
  • Democrats also nominated progressive Matt Little to replace Craig in Congress.

Results from other closely watched races Tuesday:

  • In South Carolina, Trump-endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, who replaced her brother Lindsey Graham after his death last month, advanced to an Aug. 25 GOP runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman for a full six-year term.
  • Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar easily won the Democratic primary for governor and will face state House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who defeated Trump-endorsed Mike Lindell for the GOP nomination.
  • Rep. John Larson (D-Conn.), 78, a 14-term incumbent, lost to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, who called for generational change. Larson is the seventh House Democrat and 10th House member ousted in a primary this year.

Zoom in: Wisconsin Democrats now have to unite after the party establishment's successful last-minute scramble to stop Francesca Hong, a socialist who captured the support of many young people and activists.

  • Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers endorsed Crowley as a panic broke out among many in the party that Hong could doom their chances in the fall.
  • Some Democratic voters Axios talked to were ticked off at the move. "I mean, is he trying to sabotage us?" former state party official Marga Krumins said of Evers' warning that Hong likely couldn't defeat Tiffany.
  • Crowley explicitly campaigned on the idea that Hong was a liability in the general election, telling Axios, "People don't like socialists" and "socialists didn't poll very good."
  • Hong's past social media posts, including calls to "cancel Thanksgiving" and defund the police, dominated her campaign's final week.

More takeaways from Wisconsin:

  1. Wisconsin's November election will be historic. The GOP's nominee, Rep. Tom Tiffany, would be the first person who voted to overturn the 2020 presidential results to become governor of a top swing state if he won. And Crowley would be the first Black governor in Wisconsin history.
  2. Tiffany is trying to soften his rough edges, branding himself as a "girl dad" who grew up "milking cows on a Wisconsin dairy farm." He's campaigning with former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. But now that Crowley has won, Republicans have an opponent they appear to have feared: A GOP group spent millions on ads propping up Hong, suggesting they viewed her as the weaker candidate.
  3. Tiffany could help unite Democrats. The way some progressive Democrats see it, they might have wanted Hong, but they can't risk Tiffany being governor in the 2028 presidential race given his efforts to overturn the 2020 election and his false claims there had been "hundreds of thousands of illegal votes" in Wisconsin. On the other hand, some Hong supporters are sure to be disillusioned.
  4. Hong fell short as her controversial posts surfaced and progressive leaders gave her the cold shoulder. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez declined to endorse her. And as we followed her on the campaign trail, voters clearly had electability on their minds: She was asked at stop after stop about her former comments and how she would defeat Tiffany in the fall.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly defeated socialist Francesca Hong by about 3,000 votes, dealing a blow to the progressive left's momentum Tuesday in Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, after his own polling indicated he was behind by nearly 20 points.

Why it matters: Crowley's win could breathe new life into a center-left that had been losing primary after primary in recent months, from last week's Senate contest in Michigan to House races across the country.

Yes, but: The day wasn't a total loss for progressives.

  • In the day's other big ideological showdown between Democrats, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive, defeated moderate Rep. Angie Craig in Minnesota's Senate primary by 20 points.
  • Flanagan will face GOP nominee Michele Tafoya, a former NFL TV reporter, in November.
  • Democrats also nominated progressive Matt Little to replace Craig in Congress.

Results from other closely watched races Tuesday:

  • In South Carolina, Trump-endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, who replaced her brother Lindsey Graham after his death last month, advanced to an Aug. 25 GOP runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman for a full six-year term.
  • Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar easily won the Democratic primary for governor and will face state House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who defeated Trump-endorsed Mike Lindell for the GOP nomination.

item.title: AI brings savings to clinical trials: study
item.description:
Artificial intelligence isn't just speeding up early-stage drug development, it's starting to unlock millions of dollars' worth of new efficiencies in clinical trials on cancer treatments, research shared first with Axios shows.

Why it matters: AI-powered tools could shave months off time-consuming processes like recruiting and enrolling patients, monitoring results and interpreting data.

  • That could free up resources for more clinical studies and possibly lower the high failure rate for new drugs.

What they found: A new Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development analysis found AI agents can accelerate clinical development of cancer drugs by approximately 10 weeks and reduce direct operating costs by as much as $5.6 million in late-stage trials.

  • The efficiencies increase with the number of tumors a drug can target: An experimental treatment with 50 active uses could see net benefits of as much as $565 million, Tufts found.
  • Tufts applied a clinical monitoring agent from Medable, which provides a platform to support clinical trials, to an unspecified oncology drug development program in phase 2 and 3 trials.

What they're saying: Ken Getz, the Tufts center's executive director, said deploying the agent led to new efficiencies, such as reducing the number of on-site visits, accelerating enrollment in the trial and locking in the data.

  • "To our knowledge, this is the first time that [predictive] modeling based on actual use and benchmark data has been applied to quantify the net financial impact of an agentic AI solution in a drug development program," he said.

Between the lines: AI agents could become standard features of some clinical trials in three to five years, according to Medable officials, operating like self-driving cars to tackle the grinding but necessary record-keeping that accompanies an application for new drug approval.

  • They also could be used to track the diversity of the trial population — a common concern that helps ensure an experimental treatment works for the broad population.
  • Medable officials also say the technology will enable clinical trial researchers to understand the safety and effectiveness of a drug earlier — allowing them to focus on more strategic work in drug development.
  • That's especially important in cancer drug trials, typically some of the most complex trials with some of the biggest monitoring budgets.

Reality check: AI still doesn't guarantee a trial will be a success. Some of the big challenges don't involve information processing, but revolve around finding the right patients, getting their consent and making and distributing the drug.

  • Humans also would presumably have to verify the AI agent's work, which could offset some of the overall time savings.

item.title: Anthropic's text watermarks signal new front in AI detection
item.description:
Anthropic's new models will add machine-readable "watermarks" to Claude-generated text and files to comply with new European Union transparency regulations.

Why it matters: Comms teams using Claude to simply clean up, translate, or format human-drafted press releases could stamp those documents with an AI signature.

How it works: For models launched in the EU after Aug. 2, Anthropic is marking content in two ways, "wherever Claude is offered, worldwide."

  • Text watermarks: Claude embeds patterns into the generated text that Anthropic claims are "imperceptible."
  • File metadata: Generated media files carry digital signatures confirming the asset was processed by Claude.

Yes, but: Anthropic highlighted two major limitations to its detection tech.

  • AI-assisted can look AI-generated: Content may trigger a detected mark even if Claude was used solely to proofread, format or translate human-written copy.
  • Detection drop-off: If text is heavily rewritten, mixed with other copy or too short, then the watermarks might not be detectable.

Zoom out: Anthropic explained its changes are designed to meet Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which mandates AI disclosures for generated or manipulated content.

  • OpenAI similarly outlined its compliance approach, though its current watermarking efforts primarily focus on images and audio rather than text.
  • The moves mark a regulatory-driven turn in the ongoing effort to help audiences identify AI-generated text, audio and visual content.
  • Digital platforms have recently accelerated their own AI identification measures: LinkedIn is testing a "seems like AI slop" button, Substack embedded Pangram's AI detection suite, and Snap stopped promoting AI-generated video in its main feed.

What's next: AI providers have until Dec. 2 to bring legacy models into compliance with EU rules, meaning we'll get a clearer picture in the coming months of how the industry's biggest players plan to mark AI-generated content.

item.title: Moderate Crowley narrowly beats democratic socialist Hong in Wisconsin
item.description:
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly defeated state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, in Tuesday's Wisconsin Democratic primary for governor, the Associated Press reports.

Why it matters: Hong's loss blunts progressives' recent momentum and hands moderate Democrats a chance to prove their electability in a crucial battleground state in November

  • Crowley will vie to become Wisconsin's first Black governor.

Driving the news: Crowley managed to edge out Hong by about 3,000 votes Tuesday, with 98% of the votes counted.

Zoom out: The chaotic primary left moderate Democrats fractured, as some pursued other offices and others ended their campaigns over fundraising problems, lack of support or personal scandals.

  • Hong made her working-class background central to her pitch to voters: A single mom and longtime service worker, she dropped out of college to cook full-time, rising from dishwasher to executive chef before co-owning a restaurant that closed in 2024 after years of financial strain that began during the pandemic.
  • She faced scrutiny over past positions and social media posts she later walked back, including calls to defund the police and criticism of Thanksgiving as a racist holiday.
  • Crowley similarly leaned on his own hardscrabble Milwaukee story: His family was once homeless, and he rose from community organizer to state lawmaker and eventually county executive.

The intrigue: Hong fell short without the traditional heavyweight endorsements from the left's biggest stars.

  • Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez declined to endorse Hong, focusing instead on congressional races.
  • Her opponent, Crowley, was backed by the state's top Democrat, Gov. Tony Evers, who said he offered Democrats their best chance to win.

Zoom out: Republicans were eager to run against Hong in November. Democrats said the Republican Governors Association's millions in ads served to boost Hong.

  • The bet didn't produce Republicans' preferred matchup.

What we're watching: Crowley will face Trump-endorsed Rep. Tom Tiffany in November, the Republican nominee.

  • Tiffany voted against certifying former President Biden's 2020 wins in Arizona and Pennsylvania, backed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Wisconsin and other states from casting their Electoral College votes and has continued to question Biden's victory.
  • Wisconsin's governor plays a role in certifying presidential and U.S. Senate election result, raising fears about how Tiffany could use the office if another close election is contested.

Go deeper: Bernie's revolution gets a test run for 2028 in Michigan and Wisconsin

item.title: "Woke 1 was crazy": AOC seeks do-over on 2020-era rhetoric
item.description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is trying to pull off a political feat for the ages: bury a chapter of left-wing politics that seemed like a good idea to many liberals at the time — but not so much anymore.

Why it matters: The country's most prominent democratic socialist is essentially seeking a mulligan for candidates who embraced policies like defunding the police, saying candidates should be judged on their current platforms.

  • But that will be a tough sell with moderate Democrats, let alone Republicans, in competitive races outside of blue bastions.

Driving the news: In an interview on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday, AOC was asked about some of the positions democratic socialists took around 2020. They were, she said, a product of the time.

  • "Woke 1 was crazy," she laughed, quoting a politician-friend. "And I think that what's important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now."
  • Though policy discussions around the start of the pandemic were "fruitful" given the dire straits the country was in, the "rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today," she added.

Flashback: One high-profile candidate already tried to wipe her 2020 record clean, to no avail: Kamala Harris in the last presidential election.

  • During her short-lived 2020 presidential campaign, Harris endorsed taxpayer-funded, medically necessary gender transition surgeries for federal inmates; decriminalizing border crossings; and banning plastic straws, among other things.
  • Four years later, when she replaced President Biden on the ballot, Harris tried to reposition herself as a more traditional center-left candidate. But the Trump campaign made sure voters didn't forget the past.

The other side: The problem with dismissing 2020 leftist politics as crazy in hindsight is there were plenty of Democrats who warned in real time it was crazy.

  • That list was topped by Joe Biden, who went on to win the primary and then the presidency on a center-left platform.

What they're saying: "AOC is a savvy politician. It's good she recognizes that positions she and others took on police in 2020 were bad substantively, and really bad politically," said Matt Bennett, a cofounder of the centrist Democratic group Third Way. "The problem is that some people running now are running on ideas that are even worse."

  • He mentioned Wisconsin gubernatorial hopeful Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who once called for eliminating the police as well as prisons, and even proposed doing away with Thanksgiving — all ideas she has since walked back.
  • Third Way announced last week a $15 million effort to wage "war" on the democratic socialist wing of the party.

The big picture: AOC's "Woke 1 was crazy" explanation looks like an attempt to redefine democratic socialism — distancing it from cultural and social positions that are hard to defend now and moving toward a populist economic agenda with broader appeal.

  • Her own political future — whether it's a Senate run or a presidential campaign in 2028 — could be the ultimate test of that effort.

The bottom line: There's no statute of limitations on unpopular political stands.

item.title: Rep. John Larson ouster makes 2026 a record year for Democratic primary losses
item.description:
Rep. John Larson (D-Conn.) was unseated Tuesday by his primary challenger, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, according to the Associated Press.

Why it matters: Larson is the 7th House Democrat ousted in their primary this year. Only one other election cycle in the 21st century has seen this many incumbent losses in primaries.

  • Bronin's challenge to Larson came after the 78-year-old incumbent suffered a widely publicized freeze-up during a House floor speech that he later said was the result of a complex partial seizure.
  • Bronin earned the support of the state Democratic Party, while Larson had the backing of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and the rest of Connecticut's congressional delegation.

State of play: Bronin, 47, proved to be a prodigious fundraiser, bringing in $3.1 million as of July 22 to Larson's $2.7 million over the same period, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

  • Bronin also had the most support from an outside backer: VoteVets, a group that works to elect Democratic military veterans, said in FEC filings it spent over $1 on ads boosting the retired Navy intelligence officer.
  • Larson's top outside spender was Defend the Vote, a Democratic group whose stated mission is to elect a "pro-democracy" majority in Congress. They spent just over $500,000.

Between the lines: Bronin ran a campaign that focused heavily on the need for generational change in Congress and the Democratic Party.

  • "John Larson is a good man, but he's been in Congress since the 90s. The stakes are just too high to keep doing the same thing," Bronin said in one ad.
  • Both men also tried to burnish their progressive credentials at a time when Democrats are increasingly favoring progressives in safe-seat primaries.
  • The progressive Working Families Party, which spent about $50,000 supporting Larson, ran an ad labeling Bronin a "corporate Democrat" who was "using us for political ambition."

Zoom out: Larson is part of a growing cohort of older Democrats who have lost to significantly younger primary opponents this year, including Reps. Al Green (D-Texas), Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) and Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.).

  • While DeGette, Espaillat and Thanedar all lost to challengers who ran to their left, Green and Larson both positioned themselves as stalwart progressives against opponents who focused on their age.
  • Reps. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.) and Mike Thompson (D-Calif.) both face November run-offs with younger Democratic rivals.
  • Other members who are 70 or older, including Reps. Ed Case (D-Hawaii) and Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), were able to fend off their younger primary opponents.

item.title: It's official: Amy Klobuchar is Democrats' pick to succeed Gov. Tim Walz
item.description:
U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar sailed to victory in Minnesota's Democratic primary for governor on Tuesday.

The big picture: Polling indicates that the four-term senator and 2020 presidential candidate will be a formidable contender in Democrats' bid to hold the open seat this November.

Catch up quick: Klobuchar entered the race in late January, shortly after Gov. Tim Walz reversed course and scrapped plans to run for a third term.

  • Walz's exit came amid mounting scrutiny over his administration's response to fraud targeting state social services programs.

Between the lines: The late entry into the race — and track record of out-performing other Democrats statewide — helped Klobuchar avoid a serious primary challenge from the left.

  • If she wins in November, Klobuchar will be the state's first female governor.

What's next: Summer polls showed Klobuchar with a comfortable lead over all of her potential rivals, though her support was lower than the margins of victory for her recent U.S. Senate wins.

The big picture: Polling indicates that the four-term senator and 2020 presidential candidate will be a formidable contender in Democrats' bid to hold the open seat this November.

Catch up quick: Klobuchar entered the race in late January, shortly after Gov. Tim Walz reversed course and scrapped plans to run for a third term.

  • Walz's exit came amid mounting scrutiny over his administration's response to fraud targeting state social services programs.

Between the lines: The late entry into the race — and track record of out-performing other Democrats statewide — helped Klobuchar avoid a serious primary challenge from the left.

  • If she wins in November, Klobuchar will be the state's first female governor.

What's next: Summer polls showed Klobuchar with a comfortable lead over all of her potential rivals, though her support was lower than the margins of victory for her recent U.S. Senate wins.
